title: Constructing Low‐Friction Ion Transport Pathways in Crosslinked Polymer Electrolyte for Practical Quasi‐Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT Quasi‐solid‐state polymer electrolytes are promising candidates for lithium metal batteries (LMBs) with high energy density, but still suffer from sacrificed ionic conductivity caused by electrolyte solidification. Here, by tuning monomer structures with different Li + ‐affinity, we investigate the decisive role of the segmental solvation ability of the polymer matrix in cation transport. Owing to the overly strong affinity for cations, conventional ether segments significantly decrease the Li + relaxation rate, and the resulting “sticky” polymer chains impede Li + migration. In contrast, the weakly coordinating segments such as fluorinated ether could effectively minimize coupling with Li + ions, thereby constructing “low‐friction” cation transport pathways in crosslinked polymer electrolytes, as reflected by the nearly unchanged Li + relaxation kinetics and high ionic conductivity. Therefore, the industrial Li metal pouch cells achieve excellent comprehensive electrochemical performance under harsh lean‐electrolyte conditions, with electrolyte dosage even as low as 1.3 g Ah −1 . The 2 Ah NCM811/Li cell exhibits an extended lifespan beyond 520 cycles and maintains stable operation across a wide temperature range from −50°C to +90°C. The 8.7 Ah NCM955/Li cell delivers 550 Wh kg −1 energy density and demonstrates impressive cycling stability over 260 cycles. This work could inspire fundamental understanding and further development toward practical LMBs.

title: An Engineered Thio‐Amino Polymer Achieves Potent, Safe, and Broad Cell Type Delivery in the Lung Mapped by Spatial Transcriptomics
abstract: ABSTRACT Efficient delivery of nucleic acids to the lung has the potential to impact future respiratory treatments. Current formulations exhibit significant limitations, including insufficient potency, single‐cell delivery characterizations, efficacy demonstrations in disease models, and toxicology assessments. Here we describe polymer 81 (P81), which, when used with hypotonic solvents, is 34.1‐ to 77.8‐fold more potent than previous polymers with various cargos for lung transfection by nebulized mRNA. Through the exploration of multiple routes of administration, P81 demonstrated a wide of range of cell‐type delivery, including bronchial airway epithelial cells, tracheal basal stem cells, and 54% of all cells in the distal lung, assessed via single‐cell spatial transcriptomics. Robust expression of mRNA‐encoded antibodies in the lung by P81 enabled quantification of target protein and successful suppression of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. The toxicology assessments of multiple doses of P81 polyplexes via nebulization in rodents were unremarkable. Overall, P81 represents a step forward for inhaled nucleic acid delivery to the respiratory tract, positioning itself as an efficient, safe, and translatable delivery formulation.

title: In Situ Topological Dealloying Enables Atomically Coupled Metal‐Oxide Heterostructures
abstract: ABSTRACT Metal‐oxide heterostructures are central to energy conversion and electronic devices because interfaces can modulate the configuration coupling among charge, spin, and orbit. However, conventional synthesis routes suffer from structural incompatibility and weak coupling, which hinder the universal construction of atomically coupled metal‐oxide heterointerfaces. Here, we develop an in situ topological dealloying strategy to construct metal‐oxide heterostructures with atomically interconnected interfaces. This strategy can be broadly applied to perovskite, spinel, columbite, and vanadate oxides, which enables the spontaneous formation of high‐density magnetic nanoalloys embedded within dielectric oxide matrices. Direct nanoscale visualizations of electric and magnetic fields reveal the coexistence of interfacial charge polarization and vortex‐like spin textures. These emergent dielectric and magnetic behaviors arise from atomically interfacial hybridization that mediates strong charge–spin interactions. When integrated into flexible architectures, these heterostructures exhibit broadband GHz‐frequency absorption (effective absorption bandwidth up to 6.6 GHz at 3.0 mm), high efficiency, and rapid electromagnetic‐to‐thermal energy conversion under microwave irradiation. This work establishes a general route to engineer metal‐oxide heterostructures for functional applications.

title: Scalable Hydrogel‐Programmed Porous Photonic Cement for Passive Daytime Cooling
abstract: ABSTRACT Cement is among the most widely produced materials on Earth, yet its strong solar absorption causes building envelopes to act as heat sources, increasing cooling energy demand. Here, we structurally program cement hydration to transform conventional cementitious materials into passive cooling interfaces. Through hydrogel‐confined mineralization of cement clinker, we construct a robust, hierarchically porous calcium–silicate–hydrate (C–S–H) network that integrates broadband light scattering, vapor transport and thermal insulation. By regulating the composition and crystallinity of the hydrates, the material achieves ∼95% solar reflectance and ∼98% infrared emissivity without the use of additional photonic fillers. The hygroscopic nature of the network further enables sustained evaporative cooling under humid or cloudy conditions where radiative cooling alone becomes inefficient. Life‐cycle analysis indicates that this strategy provides a pathway to transform high‐emission cement into carbon‐mitigating materials integrated within opaque building envelopes, enabling the scalable deployment of daytime radiative cooling across the built environment.

title: A Coaxial Bioprinted Hydrogel With Semipermeable Sheath and Pro‐Chondrogenic Core for Articular Cartilage Repair
abstract: ABSTRACT Stem cell‐laden hydrogels represent a promising strategy for the functional repair of articular cartilage defects. However, the pathological joint microenvironment is often characterized by persistently elevated levels of pro‐inflammatory cytokines, which severely compromise transplanted cell survival and impair their chondrogenic differentiation potential. Inspired by the hierarchical mechanical gradient of native cartilage, we developed a sheath‐core biomimetic hydrogel (SC GAE ) via embedded coaxial bioprinting, featuring a robust poly(ethylene glycol)‐alginate (PA) sheath that spatially integrates mechanical support and immunoprotection around a soft, bioactive gelatin methacryloyl‐alginate‐decellularized extracellular matrix (GAE) core. The dense PA sheath provides immediate mechanical support and functions as a size‐selective diffusion barrier, permitting nutrient and oxygen permeation while effectively blocking inflammatory cytokines (>40 kDa). This protective niche enables the pericellular matrix‐mimicking GAE core to maintain stem cell viability >89% under pro‐inflammatory conditions and support robust chondrogenic differentiation. In a rabbit osteochondral defect model, bone marrow stromal cell‐laden SC GAE constructs promoted substantial cartilage repair, achieving defect filling, host integration, and regeneration of glycosaminoglycan‐rich hyaline‐like cartilage. This sheath‐core architecture design spatially integrates structural, mechanical, and immunoprotection functions, presenting a promising platform for the regeneration of load‐bearing articular cartilage.

title: Staged Network Evolution Enables In Situ Strengthening and On‐Demand Recyclability of Polyurethanes via Dynamic Sulfilimine–Urea Bonds
abstract: ABSTRACT Cross‐linked polymers exhibit exceptional mechanical robustness, dimensional stability, and chemical resistance arising from permanent covalent networks. However, it remains challenging to tune mechanical properties after curing and to decouple on‐demand recyclability from in‐use stability. Herein, we report a staged network evolution strategy based on dynamic sulfilimine–urea bonds to address these demands. The rapid room‐temperature addition of isocyanates to sulfilimines forms dynamic sulfilimine–urea linkages, affording a solvent‐resistant initial polyurethane (SUP‐S1). Subsequent thermal treatment of SUP‐S1 induces dissociation of the sulfilimine–urea linkages, regenerating the sulfilimine motifs and releasing isocyanates that are captured in situ by backbone hydroxyl groups to form thermodynamically stable urethane bonds. The tensile strength and toughness of the obtained polyurethane (SUP‐S2) are significantly enhanced, increasing from 17 to 42 MPa and from 55 to 158 MJ m −3 , respectively, while the Young's modulus is retained. Moreover, the photoclip of sulfilimine motifs facilitates on‐demand recyclability by reducing the cross‐link density. The resulting recyclable polyurethane (SUP‐S3) exhibits excellent multi‐recyclability, retaining over 96% of its mechanical properties after five recycling cycles. This staged network evolution design reconciles the enhancement of mechanical properties with end‐of‐life recyclability within a single material platform, providing a robust pathway for the development of next‐generation sustainable cross‐linked polymeric materials.

title: A Janus Bilayer Portland Cement‐Based Moisture‐Electricity Generator via Hydrogen‐Bonding Network Regulation
abstract: ABSTRACT The ubiquitous interaction between ambient moisture and built environments presents a compelling opportunity for continuous energy harvesting through moisture‐electricity generation (MEG). However, current MEG materials fail to satisfy high‐power demands in buildings because hydrogen bonds, indispensable for the structural integrity of soft carbon‐chain networks, severely restrict water diffusion, and thus bottleneck MEG performance. Hydrated Portland cement, featuring a robust silicate backbone, allows aggressive modulation of the water hydrogen‐bonding network (HBN), emerging as an ideal platform for higher performance. Here, we developed a Portland cement‐based moisture‐electricity generator (CMEG) via a facile asymmetric acid etching strategy, extending MEG to cementitious material systems. The resulting CMEG presents a Janus bilayer architecture with a stark gradient in hygroscopicity across the layers to drive the unidirectional diffusion of water molecules. Mechanistically, the etching process induces the breakage of HBN, which unlocks ultrafast water diffusion throughout the top layer and thus accelerates selective ion transport toward the bottom layer. Remarkably, CMEG delivers an extremely high short‐circuit current density of 723 µA/cm 2 and output power density of 112.5 µW/cm 2 . Furthermore, CMEG demonstrates exceptional scalability, modular integration capabilities and nearly identical mechanical strength to that before acid etching, proving its giant potential for future self‐powered buildings and infrastructures.

title: Deciphering Roles of Interfacial Tunable Primer for High Active Material Contents Pure Silicon Electrodes
abstract: Abstract While pure silicon (Si) is a highly attractive anode material for next‐generation high‐energy‐density lithium‐ion batteries, its practical implementation is limited by severe volumetric fluctuations during cycling. This intrinsic instability inevitably induces continuous structural degradation, strictly restricting the maximum allowable active material fraction within the electrode. To address this critical challenge, we design an interfacial tunable functional primer ( fp ) that serves as an effective multi‐component bridging agent. By optimizing the mechanical resilience and electrochemical cohesion among electrode components, the fp layer dissipates interfacial stress and secures continuous electron conduction pathways. Furthermore, the unique ionophoric properties of the benzoxazine framework directly regulate the interfacial solvation structure and enhance ion flux. Driven by these integrated effects, the fp ‐modified Si anode achieves remarkable electrochemical reversibility even at a nearly binder‐free composition containing 99 wt% active material content. This strategy completely averts the rapid physical degradation typically observed in standard binder networks under such extreme formulations. Furthermore, fp ‐modified Si demonstrates practical viability by assembling double‐stacked pouch cells paired with NCM90 cathodes, which exhibit long‐term cycle durability. This study provides a highly effective paradigm for electrode‐component regulation and molecular‐level engineering in pure Si anode interfacial modification strategies.

title: Intranasal Pathogenesis‐Adaptive Nanotherapeutics Reinstate Regenerative Competence for Post‐Stroke Neural Repair
abstract: ABSTRACT Poststroke neurorehabilitation is limited by the poor regenerative capacity of adult neurons. Although neural stem cells (NSCs) can generate new neurons, their reparative potential is constrained by inefficient delivery to cerebral lesions and a hostile regenerative niche. Here, analysis of a single‐nucleus transcriptomic dataset revealed pronounced dysfunction and intercellular crosstalk among neurons, microglia, and NSCs, highlighting redox imbalance and impaired nitric oxide (NO) signaling as potential therapeutic targets. Guided by these findings, we develop FCeO 2 @GLp, a pathogenesis‐adaptive nanotherapeutic integrating reactive oxygen species scavenging, NO replenishment and immune modulation within cerebral ischemic microenvironment. Following intranasal administration, FCeO 2 @GLp actively adheres to the olfactory epithelium (OE), reaches infarcted brain regions, releases cerium oxide (CeO 2 ) nanozyme, fingolimod, and a NO donor in response to local acidity. This coordinated strategy alleviates oxidative stress, reprograms microglia, protects neurons, and enhances NSC proliferation and neuronal differentiation. Consequently, FCeO 2 @GLp effectively reduces infarct volume and cerebral edema during the acute phase, and improves long‐term neurological function and survival, establishing a lesion‐responsive strategy for poststroke neural repair.

title: Bridge‐Level Electronic Compensation in Prussian White Cathodes: Charge‐Transfer Kinetic Regimes and Design Principles
abstract: ABSTRACT Prussian White (PW) cathodes are promising sodium–ion battery materials because of their open framework, low cost, and high structural reversibility. However, polarization and capacity loss under high‐rate or low‐temperature operation arise from coupled ionic, structural, interfacial, and electronic processes that are not fully captured by Na + diffusion or average structural evolution alone. This perspective introduces a bridge‐level electronic‐compensation framework in which the Fe─C≡N─TM bridge is treated as a local unit for describing local charge redistribution. Using Marcus‐type descriptors together with concepts of metal‐to‐metal charge transfer, intervalence charge transfer, and metal–ligand interactions, three physical contributions are emphasized: the local charge‐state free‐energy difference ( ΔG° ), cyanide‐mediated electronic coupling ( H ab ), and structure‐coupled reorganization energy ( λ ). Local bridge states are organized into descriptor‐based kinetic regimes based on the balance among energetic mismatch, electronic coupling, and structural reorganization, with transition‐metal chemistries serving as representative mechanistic cases. These descriptors are further translated into design principles involving redox‐level alignment, cyanide‐mediated coupling and network connectivity, and control of local structural reorganization. This perspective provides a physical basis for interpreting bridge‐level electronic compensation and considering how local energetic alignment, coupling, and structural reorganization can be regulated in PW cathodes.

title: Synergistic Dual‐Site Regulation in a Tailored Imine‐COF for Enhanced Hydrogen Peroxide Photosynthesis
abstract: ABSTRACT Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) emerge as promising candidates for the photocatalytic production of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ). However, precise modulation of the chemical environment of active sites in COFs remains a significant challenge. Based on a molecular engineering strategy, this study focuses on hierarchical regulation of nitrogen coordination environments for efficient photocatalytic H 2 O 2 production through the 2e − ORR. Intrinsic nitrogen configurations (triazine vs. pyridine) are first tailored to construct two types of COFs. The pyridyl‐imine TAPT‐BTPA ( 4 ) optimizes charge carrier separation and extends visible‐light absorption, leading to an enhanced H 2 O 2 production rate of 8.12 mmol g −1 h −1 in aqueous solution containing isopropanol as a sacrificial agent under an O 2 atmosphere. Main‐group metals (In, Sn, and Sb) are then anchored at the pyridine‐imine sites to modulate local electron density further and steer reaction pathways. Structural characterization and activity tests reveal that Sb‐coordinated TAPT‐BTPA‐Sb ( 10 ) induces a unique synergistic effect, redirecting the ORR toward a more favorable stepwise 1e − route. This significant pathway regulation ultimately boosts the H 2 O 2 production rate to 15.3 mmol g −1 h −1 under the same conditions. This work clarifies the decisive role of coordination environment engineering and establishes a molecular‐level design paradigm for advanced H 2 O 2 synthesis photocatalysts.

title: Cocrystals for sequestering and separating large PAHs
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Highly adaptive boroxine organic assemblies (BOAs) derived from a boronic acid and a linear alkene function as a first-generation constitutional dynamic library (CDL) to sequester and separate large polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in form of cocrystals. Configurational and conformational isomerism of the organoboroxines in host-guest assemblies is induced by electronic properties, shape and size of the PAHs through a “shrink-wrap” process/mechanism, which reveals a templating role of the PAH during the CDL assembly. The CDL was applied to separate up to three different PAHs. The cocrystals exhibit tunable electronic properties. The CDL afforded a cocrystal wherein alkenes of two different BOAs undergo [2 + 2] photocycloaddition in the same solid.

title: Single-cell profiling of the duodenum during chronic human norovirus infection
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Human noroviruses are a major cause of diarrheal disease, yet their pathogenesis remains poorly defined. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of duodenal biopsies and matched stem cell–derived enteroids from immunodeficient individuals with chronic norovirus infection. Norovirus RNA was detected primarily in enterocytes, enteroendocrine cells, and macrophages, with the highest proportion of viral RNA-positive cells observed among M2 macrophages, followed by late enterocytes. Despite this distribution, late enterocytes produced higher viral yields than differentiated M2 macrophages in vitro. Norovirus infection was associated with the up-regulation of MHC class I-related genes and
                    IL15
                    in duodenal macrophages and late enterocytes, together with increased
                    IFNG
                    expression by CD8 T cells. Macrophages and late enterocytes up-regulated
                    CXCL9
                    and
                    CXCL10/11
                    , respectively, consistent with CD8 and CD4 T cell recruitment to the duodenum. These findings show that noroviruses infect and persist across multiple permissive cell types during chronic infection, resulting in marked dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses that may drive pathogenesis.

title: Boosting stability and charge transfer of conducting polymer poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO) through complementary topology
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO) is a benchmark n-type conjugated polymer known for its record-high electrical conductivity. Nevertheless, its thermal robustness and charge/ion transport characteristics remain insufficient. To address this issue, we report a hierarchical complementary topology strategy via doping PBFDO with choline chloride (ChCl). At the molecular scale, the cations Ch
                    +
                    selectively intercalate along the out-of-plane direction while simultaneously densifying the in-plane π-π stacking, accompanied by partial removal of H
                    +
                    . At the submicrometer scale, this induces distinct phase separation into high- and low-density stacking domains. As a result, the product PBFDO-ChCl exhibited a synergistic performance boost, with a 2.8-fold enhancement in high-temperature resilience, a 1.6-fold increase in sheet conductance, and a 15.9-fold reduction in ion diffusion resistance. Then, organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) using PBFDO-ChCl as channel material further confirm these performance enhancements. As a whole, this work closes the performance gap between n-type PBFDO and state-of-the-art p-type conjugated polymers, potentially advancing its applications from energy storage to bioelectronics and neuromorphic computing.

title: Segmented projection image translation for large-area, high-resolution vat photopolymerization
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: High-resolution projection-based vat photopolymerization (VP) 3D printing enables rapid fabrication of highly detailed polymeric structures. However, expanding the build area traditionally compromises resolution, creating a fundamental trade-off between projected pixel size and printable area due to fixed digital micromirror device (DMD) pixel counts. Herein, we introduce segmented projection image translation (SPIN), a simple implementation strategy that expands the effective projection area by applying controlled orbital translation to an off-axis objective lens within the optical infinity space. In this work, we demonstrate a projection-based VP printer implemented with SPIN that expands the effective build area by 4.8-fold, from a native field of 60.4 square millimeters to an expanded domain of 290.5 square millimeters. The SPIN-enabled printer produces isolated line features as thin as 9.8 ± 2.2 micrometers and fabricates intricate three-dimensional truss structures with features as small as 30 micrometers. These results validate a practical route for extending microscale projection-based VP printing to larger build areas while preserving feature fidelity across stitched exposure fields.

title: Dual-action small-molecule VSP-51-2 ameliorates polycystic ovary syndrome via PPARγ modulation and AKR1C3 inhibition
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a prevalent multifactorial endocrine disorder, is inadequately managed by current therapies that fail to concurrently target its core metabolic (insulin resistance) and reproductive (hyperandrogenism) pathologies. We report VSP-51-2, a dual-target lead compound initially engineered as a selective PPARγ modulator that unexpectedly exerts potent uncompetitive inhibition of the androgen-synthesizing enzyme AKR1C3 through a putative allosteric mechanism. In preclinical PCOS models, VSP-51-2 restored regular estrous cyclicity, improved ovarian follicular morphology, enhanced systemic insulin sensitivity, suppressed hyperandrogenism, and did not significantly perturb measured hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis hormonal parameters. Mechanistically, it blocks PPARγ phosphorylation at Ser
                    273
                    , thereby enhancing adiponectin secretion and GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake, and is predicted to bind a putative allosteric pocket of AKR1C3 to constrain androgen biosynthesis. These findings support VSP-51-2 as a preclinical proof-of-concept compound for a dual-target strategy that addresses metabolic dysfunction and androgen excess through a unified molecular scaffold.

title: Multimodal switches exploiting electromechanical snap-through for versatile robotic information processing
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: It is highly desirable to design and engineer lightweight, low-power-consumption, and rapid physical intelligence (PI) structures that couple with multiple robotic functions. Here, we present a multimodal electromechanical switch (mEMS), consisting of a stretchable droplet-amplified electrostatic zipping structure, a convex bump, and a pair of electrical contacts, that can be used to achieve the widely used mechanical momentary, mechanical latching, and electrically actuated switching modes by simply tuning the applied voltage and using the same structure. We theoretically investigate the snap-through behavior of the elastic zipping membrane, which can be used to endow the mEMS with voltage-dependent memory, and the theoretical considerations are experimentally validated. As a result, we can apply the mEMS array for robotic memory, such as information writing and erasing; robotic communication by reprogrammable information encrypting, decrypting, and display; robotic computation by electrically reprogrammable logic gates; and reprogrammable binary information transferring. The mEMS represents a comprehensive PI structure for next-generation autonomous machines that can better adapt in unstructured and complex real-world environments.

title: Real-time complex-valued RF blind source separation via in-physics computing
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The rise of edge-centric 6G networks demands real-time intelligent processing of heterogeneous radio-frequency (RF) signals. Complex-valued blind source separation (CV-BSS) provides a physical-layer capability, enabling the blind extraction of source components from overlapping RF signals. Here, we demonstrate an integrated photonic vector processor (IPVP) that implements real-time CV-BSS via in-physics computation directly on raw RF signals. The IPVP operates across multiple RF bands up to 24 GHz and achieves blind, in-hardware adaptation to unknown sources and channels via in situ learning. Experiments demonstrate the efficacy of IPVP in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications and multi-band radar interference suppression. The IPVP reduces the EVMs of the two recovered signals from over 50% to 6.18% and 5.3%, respectively, while enhancing the SIR by up to 26 dB. This work demonstrates, to our knowledge, the first photonic processor capable of real-time CV-BSS at RF, highlighting the potential of integrated photonic hardware for ultralow-latency, edge-intelligent signal processing.

title: Controllable fabrication of visible-spectrum 3D photonic crystals
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The fabrication of visible-spectrum three-dimensional (3D) photonic crystals (PhCs) remains highly challenging, because existing manufacturing techniques cannot simultaneously achieve high processing precision and sufficient geometric freedom. Here, we propose a suspended pyrolysis-assisted two-photon polymerization (SP-TPP) printing strategy, achieving the controllable fabrication of visible-spectrum 3D PhCs. The resulting 3D diamond PhCs exhibit a remarkable lattice-period standard deviation of only 5.75 nm, approximately 1/45 of that achieved without suspended pyrolysis. Microscopic reflection spectra confirm these PhCs possess uniform optical responses across all spatial positions. By tuning the lattice period and structural duty cycle, the PhCs operating at diverse wavelengths are systematically realized. Moreover, through the demonstration of PhC prototype structures and in situ arrayed fabrication, the SP-TPP printing strategy paves the way for applications in photonic microcavities, 3D optical waveguides, optical splitters, and integrated micro-optical systems.

title: Reprogramming electron transfer at single-atom Pt sites to break the interference barrier in uric acid detection
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Uric acid (UA) serves as a key biomarker for gout, cardiovascular disease, and kidney dysfunction, yet conventional detection methods relying on H
                    2
                    O
                    2
                    generation suffer from signal instability and interference from reductive species. Here, we report a uricase-like platinum-nitrogen-carbon nanozyme (Pt-N-C-NH
                    3
                    ) that redirects UA oxidation from a two-electron pathway toward a four-electron pathway. By decreasing graphitic nitrogen content, the local electronic microenvironment of platinum sites is modulated, which is associated with a lower calculated free-energy change for the rate-determining absorbed oxygen to absorbed hydroxyl transformation from 1.25 to 0.62 electron volts and thereby promoting oxygen reduction to water. Integrated into a microneedle sensing platform, UA is converted to allantoin for chemiluminescent readout. The sensor exhibits a wide linear range of 50.00 to 1000.00 μM and a detection limit of 15.86 μM, while maintaining 97.57% signal stability against reductive interferents. This work demonstrates that atomic-level coordination engineering enables programmable control over reaction pathways in artificial enzyme systems, thereby facilitating robust biosensing in complex biological environments.

title: Nonlinear cooling and control of a mechanical quantum harmonic oscillator
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Nonlinearities are a key feature allowing nonclassical control of quantum harmonic oscillators. However, when nonlinearities are strong, designing protocols for control is often difficult, placing a barrier to exploiting these properties fully. In this work, using a single trapped-ion oscillator operated in the strongly nonlinear regime of the atom-light interaction, we show how to generate localized multi (two, three, four, and five)–component Schrödinger’s cat manifolds using a novel form of nonlinear reservoir engineering. We then specifically select Hamiltonians which allow us to perform measurements on these state manifolds. Our work demonstrates the experimental use of high-order nonlinear processes for control of nonclassical states of a quantum harmonic oscillator, opening up a new toolbox which can be applied to bosonic quantum error correction, computation, and sensing.

title: Phototropin-mediated blue light signaling orients the asymmetry of Marchantia polymorpha spores
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Multicellular organisms produced by sexual reproduction develop from single cells, and the asymmetry of these cells can define the orientation of the earliest developmental axes. The haploid multicellular stage of the plant,
                    Marchantia polymorpha,
                    develops from a single cell—the spore—that divides asymmetrically, producing an apical germ cell that generates the plant body and a smaller basal cell that differentiates as an anchoring germ rhizoid cell. We show that the orientation of this asymmetric cell division is controlled by an external environmental cue—blue light—that is perceived by the photoreceptor phototropin. This process requires the NCH1 (NRL PROTEIN FOR CHLOROPLAST MOVEMENT 1) protein for downstream signaling. Together, these findings define core elements of the mechanism by which a directional environmental signal orients cell division, which, in turn, orients the first axis of symmetry.

title: Arbitrarily cuttable and ultrathin MXene structural colors for customizable and wearable multispectral information management
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Structural colors based on natural and artificial microstructures show promising light manipulation. As atomically thick building blocks, Ti

title: Does government-assisted relocation help households
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Climate change is intensifying floods and storms, leading governments to consider relocating households away from high-risk areas. Yet, there is little evidence on whether such programs reduce risk or improve household well-being. I evaluate the US Federal Emergency Management Agency’s property acquisition (“buyout”) program using nationwide longitudinal records that track households before and after approval. By comparing households facing similar mapped flood risks, I estimate the program’s effects on relocation, residence in high-risk flood areas, and financial outcomes. Households that participate are more likely to relocate outside Federal Emergency Management Agency–designated flood hazard areas and experience short-term reductions in debt and improvements in neighborhood socioeconomic conditions. However, these benefits are concentrated among participants from wealthier and predominantly white neighborhoods, who relocate more quickly and achieve larger reductions in risk. A benefit-cost analysis shows that the program value depends on implementation costs and realized reductions in flood-risk exposure, with benefit-cost ratios ranging from 0.84 to 1.28 across three scenarios. These results show that government-assisted relocation can be an effective adaptation tool, but its social and economic benefits remain unevenly distributed.

title: Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Marine net primary production is expected to be affected by climate change. Although remote sensing offers broad spatial and temporal coverage, it is limited to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability. Autonomous profiling floats provide critical depth-resolved measurements that help bridge this gap. Here, we use data from the biogeochemical-Argo array to estimate basin-scale change in net primary production using the carbon-based production algorithm. We find statistically significant negative trends across the Atlantic and Southern Oceans and positive trends in the Pacific Ocean. These changes, if occurring in response to climate forcing, raise concern due to the key role of phytoplankton productivity in sustaining marine ecosystems. These trends typically agree in direction and magnitude with those from satellites. Our findings highlight the value of the biogeochemical-Argo array in detecting change in ocean productivity, demonstrating its potential for sustained monitoring. These results underscore the need for integrated observing systems to capture the full extent of changing marine productivity.

title: Cell adhesion molecule–related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog–producing cells
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

title: Asymmetric cell division is predictive of human T cell vaccine responses
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Vaccine-induced protection relies on the generation and maintenance of stem-like memory B and T cells, a process sustained by two conserved mechanisms: asymmetric cell division (ACD) and autophagy. In T cells, ACD enables them to produce progeny with the same T cell receptor but with divergent metabolic and functional fates upon antigen encounter through the unequal inheritance of cellular cargoes. Autophagy recycles cellular components, provides metabolic substrates essential for sustaining energy demands, and is relevant for the maintenance of T cell memory. Direct evidence of how these processes synergize and affect human immunity is still lacking. Here, we show that mitotic human CD8
                    +
                    T cells asymmetrically segregate autophagy-related organelles, including autophagosomes and lysosomes. Furthermore, we show that ACD drives divergent transcriptional and functional fates in daughter cells. Extending these findings to an influenza vaccine trial, we demonstrate that autophagic flux follows the dynamics of clonal expansion and contraction of antigen-specific T cells. Notably, individuals with enhanced ACD capacity, especially with increased LC3B asymmetry, exhibit better vaccine responses, linking early cellular segregation events to long-term immune fitness. Last, transient use of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 inhibitor rapamycin improved memory survival, which was associated with improved ACD, measured by the asymmetric inheritance of both CD8 and LC3B. Together, these findings highlight that the asymmetric inheritance of the autophagy machinery represents another layer of human adaptive immunity and offers a potential therapeutic target to enhance vaccine outcomes.

title: Piezoelectrically actuated magnetic dipole twisting resonators enable miniaturized low-frequency antennas
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Miniaturized low-frequency antennas are essential for underwater, underground, and biomedical communications, yet their performance is constrained by the fundamental size-efficiency trade-off, a long-standing physical bottleneck. Here, we introduce a radiation mechanism that circumvents this constraint by replacing the time-varying currents in conventional antennas with the mechanical twisting oscillation of a magnetic dipole. Using piezoelectrically actuated, biomimetic twisting resonators with ultrahigh mechanical quality factors, we demonstrate that low-frequency antennas operating at 15.4 and 668 hertz can be miniaturized to centimeter- and millimeter-scale, respectively, with radiation efficiencies exceeding those of size-matched loop antennas by factors of 49,000 and 5000, respectively. This electromechanical-magnetic transduction enables underwater cross-medium communication over 115 meters with only milliwatt-level power consumption, using 99.9% less power than loop antennas. It also supports implantable wireless devices that achieve a fourfold increase in communication range at identical power consumption, opening a route to long-range, low-power wireless systems capable of operating in some of the most demanding environments.

title: A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year
                    −1
                    during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

title: Structural insights into light harvesting and photosystem II evolution in the basal streptophyte Mesostigma viride
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The basal streptophyte
                    Mesostigma viride
                    represents a critical evolutionary transition toward land plants, yet the molecular basis of its ancestral light-harvesting strategy remains elusive. Here, we present a 2.25-angstrom resolution cryo-EM structure of the
                    M. viride
                    PSII-LHCII-LHCP supercomplex, revealing a unique C
                    2
                    S
                    2
                    M
                    p2
                    L
                    p2
                    -type architecture. Our structure reveals a nearly complete set of conserved PSII core subunits, indicating that much of the PSII structural framework found in terrestrial plants was established early in the streptophyte lineage. At the periphery, the complex features a specialized antenna module in which two ancestral LHCP monomers flank CP29. These ancestral antenna proteins bind an unusually high number of carotenoids, with seven carotenoids per subunit, and extensively incorporate marine-type keto carotenoids, siphonaxanthin, and siphonein, throughout the complex, thereby broadening absorption in the blue-green region. The canonical LHCII trimer exhibits a distinctive chlorophyll
                    b
                    macrocluster and a 96-femtosecond ultrafast energy transfer component. Together, these findings provide a high-resolution molecular framework for an evolutionary intermediate that combines high-capacity aquatic light harvesting with structural features potentially relevant to photoprotection during the transition toward terrestrial life.

title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid–releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

title: Weak adsorption, strong consequences: How trace gases control ice growth and quasi-liquid-layer structure
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Gases in the atmosphere are often treated as passive background species in cold environments, yet their molecular roles at icy interfaces remain poorly understood. Here, we show how hydrophobic and hydrophilic trace gases can actively reorganize the ice interface and regulate freezing through interfacial stabilization. We find these gases can actively modulate both the kinetics and thermodynamics of the water-ice interface. Using molecular simulations, we find that all gases examined retard ice-front propagation relative to pure water to different extents. This slowing arises from weak but preferential adsorption at the water-ice interface, where gases occupy water-dense interfacial layers and locally suppress ice-like ordering. After freezing is complete, gases do not distribute uniformly across the frozen surface, but partition selectively among multiple adsorption regions across the ice–quasi-liquid-layer (QLL)–air interfacial landscape. Relatively hydrophobic gases exhibit a three-region adsorption pattern, whereas relatively hydrophilic gases occupy only two dominant adsorption regions. Despite these differences, both classes preferentially accumulate near the QLL-air boundary and its immediate outer region rather than the ice-QLL interface. There, gases pair with and compensate for dangling surface bonds (through a surface-passivating effect reminiscent of ligand stabilization), reducing the thermodynamic driving force for premelting and thereby thinning the QLL. These results establish a unified molecular picture in which atmospheric gases are active interfacial modulators of both ice growth and ice structure, with implications for freezing, ice-cloud microphysics, and heterogeneous atmospheric chemistry.

title: A fully hydrogel implantable patch for in situ ultrasonic monitoring of gastric leakage
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Gastric leakage is a common and life-threatening postoperative complication, while delayed detection often leads to severe abdominal organ damage. Current radiological imaging modalities are limited in their ability to provide timely detection of gastric leakage, while the mechanical mismatch and long-term persistence of conventional electronic sensors limit their implantable applications. In this work, we developed a fully hydrogel-based ultrasonic metagel patch (USMP) for direct, real-time monitoring of gastric leakage via ultrasound imaging. The USMP incorporates a tree-ring air cell array, in which densely distributed air cells arranged in concentric rings create a strong back-scattering effect, thereby producing distinctive and stable ultrasound imaging signatures for rapid and sensitive detection. The air cells are encapsulated within biocompatible, hydrolytically degradable pH-responsive hydrogels, forming a fully hydrogel sensing architecture. The potential of the USMP for gastric leakage monitoring up to 7 days postimplantation is validated in the live rabbit model.

title: Mechanical forces enable human stem cell modeling of protein aggregation cardiomyopathy
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Inherited cardiomyopathies are the leading cause of heart failure in young adults, with limited therapeutic options. Desmin-related cardiomyopathy (DRM), caused by mutations to cytoskeletal proteins and their chaperones, exemplifies this challenge: Here, protein quality control is compromised, leading to toxic protein aggregates that destroy cardiomyocyte contractile machinery. One of the deadliest DRM mutations in the chaperone protein αB crystallin (CRYAB-R120G) lacks a genetically matched preclinical model: Mouse models require massive overexpression of mutant CRYAB, raising questions about physiological relevance. Here, we establish a human model of
                    CRYAB
                    -linked DRM, using induced pluripotent stem cells expressing CRYAB-R120G at near-endogenous levels. We show that three-dimensional mechanical loading, but not fatty acid–based metabolic maturation media, is essential for expressing Desmin, whose aggregation defines DRM. Using microengineered heart tissues, we found that contractile deficits are associated with impaired calcium handling, pointing to electromechanical uncoupling in DRM. Treatment with the Janus kinase 1 inhibitor itacitinib partially rescued contractility, providing a functional validation of this emerging therapeutic strategy.

title: Electronic hair: Transforming hair into a scalable bioelectronic interface
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: In electroencephalography, hair remains a major barrier to electrode-skin contact, limiting signal quality. Here, we introduce electronic hair (eHAIR), a strategy that converts hair into a bioelectronic interface using mixed ionic-electronic conductive polymer dyes. Hair, a keratinized filament anchored within the skin, provides a stable and naturally distributed platform for interfacing. Two complementary approaches based on polythiophene derivatives enable rapid, washable functionalization of hair bundles or semipermanent coating of individual strands. The resulting eHAIR forms conformal, low-impedance interfaces that support electrophysiological recordings with increased signal amplitude and spectral power while preserving the underlying neural dynamics without gels or rigid hardware. Beyond passive sensing, eHAIR-based organic electrochemical transistors enable local signal amplification, with gain defined by hair geometry. By repurposing hair as an active bioelectronic interface, eHAIR establishes a wearable and biointegrated platform that can be implemented from individual hairs to larger hair-covered regions.

title: The ZmJAZ14–ZmMYC2 module regulates anthesis–silking synchrony in maize
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The evolution of traits can increase yield potential but may create physiological constraints. Jasmonic acid (JA) signaling regulates sex determination in male (tassel) and female (ear) inflorescences in maize. Although the formation of ears laid the foundation for high yields, the asynchronous development of the tassel and the ear prolongs the anthesis-silking interval (ASI), threatening reproductive success and reducing yield. Whether JA signaling coordinates ear and tassel development remains unclear. Here, we show that the core JA signaling module, ZmJAZ14-ZmMYC2a/b, orchestrates the expression of
                    SPL29
                    for reproductive transition,
                    BA1
                    for female inflorescence initiation, and
                    EXPA5
                    for silk elongation. Coordination of these physiological processes underpins synchronous growth of the tassel and ears, whereas disruption of
                    ZmMYC2a/b
                    or accumulation of the repressor ZmJAZ14 prolongs ASI. Our work suggests that the repurposing of JA signaling to coordinate ear and tassel development may represent a lineage-specific evolutionary burden in maize. Deciphering the link between gains and unforeseen costs of evolution could further improve yields.

title: Tracing Neanderthal ancestry patterns through successive population expansions in Europe
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: During their expansion from Africa, modern humans interbred with Neanderthals, resulting in introgression of Neanderthal DNA into their genomes. This process contributed to a Southeast-to-Northwest gradient of Neanderthal ancestry across Europe. We investigate the population dynamics underlying the emergence and persistence of this gradient through two successive human range expansions. We developed a three-population, layered, spatially explicit simulation framework to track the spatiotemporal evolution of Neanderthal ancestry under a model of interactions among Neanderthals, pre-Neolithic hunter-gatherers, and Neolithic farmers. Our results indicate that the ancestry cline emerged from the interplay between the direction of the initial hunter-gatherer expansion, the northern limit of the Neanderthal range, and strong reproductive isolation, without requiring natural selection. The similar direction of the subsequent Neolithic expansion explains the cline’s persistence and Neanderthal ancestry differences between hunter-gatherers and farmers. These findings demonstrate how spatiotemporal patterns in ancient DNA provide insights into past population dynamics.

title: Brown carbon in biomass burning aerosol enhances HONO production
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Nitrous acid (HONO) is an important source of hydroxyl radicals (•OH). •OH drives ozone and aerosol formation, affecting air quality, health, and climate. Elevated HONO concentrations have been observed in biomass burning (BB) plumes. However, the mechanism remains unclear, hindering parameterization and quantification of the impacts. Here, we conducted flow tube experiments with BB aerosol samples and proxies to investigate renoxification, a process that converts nitrate into HONO and NO
                    
                      x
                    
                    (NO and NO
                    2
                    ). Our results reveal that renoxification in BB aerosol is enhanced by brown carbon (BrC) through electron transfer to nitrate as an alternative to surface-enhanced nitrate photolysis. We develop parameterization to assess the potential global impacts of BrC-enhanced renoxification, which suggests that BrC enhances surface-level HONO production by up to one order of magnitude in BB-affected regions, with surface HONO production exceeding 1 part per trillion per hour in regions with high aerosol nitrate. These impacts are expected to worsen as BB intensifies in a warming climate.

title: Input-specific deployment of the active zone scaffold RIM tunes synaptic release probability and plasticity
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The multidomain scaffold RIM (Rab3-interacting molecule) is widely viewed as a broadly required organizer of the presynaptic active zone, clustering voltage-gated Ca
                    2+
                    (Ca
                    v
                    2) channels, priming synaptic vesicles, and supporting neurotransmitter release. Whether this reliance is uniform across synapses with distinct release probabilities, however, has been difficult to resolve at convergent inputs. Here, using neurotoxin-based silencing to isolate transmission at the
                    Drosophila
                    neuromuscular junction, we show that the requirement for RIM is highly input-specific: RIM is essential to empower transmission at a high–release probability phasic synapse, yet is largely dispensable at a neighboring low–release probability tonic synapse. This specificity extends to plasticity: RIM is required for acute homeostatic potentiation at the phasic input, but not for chronic potentiation at the tonic input. Super-resolution imaging reveals that RIM is positioned closer to Ca
                    v
                    2 channels at phasic synapses and, during acute plasticity, coordinates their nanoscale reorganization to drive the rapid expansion of the readily releasable pool.

title: A TROP2-targeting aptamer enables selective drug delivery and potent antitumor activity in pancreatic cancer
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains difficult to treat, highlighting the need for strategies that selectively deliver cytotoxic agents to tumor cells. Trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2 (TROP2) has been proposed as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC, but non-antibody-based delivery formats remain underexplored. Using protein-SELEX, we identified T17, a high-affinity aptamer that specifically binds to TROP2, and conjugated it to monomethyl auristatin E through an MC-Val-Cit-PAB linker to generate the aptamer-drug conjugate T17-M. Preclinical evaluation in cellular and animal models showed that T17-M retained TROP2-dependent binding, underwent clathrin-mediated internalization and lysosomal processing, and suppressed tumor growth in cell-line-derived and patient-derived xenografts. T17-M also reduced liver metastasis and induced calreticulin exposure, ATP release, and HMGB1 secretion, consistent with immunogenic cell death. In immunocompetent models, T17-M promoted dendritic-cell activation and CD8
                    +
                    T cell infiltration, while its combination with PD-1 blockade further enhanced tumor control and prolonged survival. These findings provide preclinical proof-of-concept for T17-M as an alternative TROP2-targeted drug-delivery strategy for PDAC.

title: The role of network connectivity and transcriptomic vulnerability in shaping gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Clinical progression is strongly linked to gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis (MS), detectable early on MRI and progressing nonrandomly across the brain. However, the mechanisms driving its spatiotemporal progression and individual variability remain unclear. Using MRIs from 2187 participants, alongside normative data, we systematically investigated network-based mechanisms underlying MS-related atrophy. Regional atrophy was associated with functional cortical hubness, supporting the nodal stress hypothesis, and was constrained by anatomical and functional connections, consistent with transneuronal degeneration. Lesional disconnection and transcriptomic vulnerability played marginal roles. Patient- and subgroup-level analyses revealed that network-based mechanisms are specifically linked to MS-related neurodegeneration and may operate differently in distinct subtypes or disease phases. Atrophy patterns were anchored to the connectivity profiles of disease epicenters involving the visual, sensorimotor, and temporal cortices, as well as the hippocampi, amygdalae, and thalami. Network-based measures enhanced the explanation of future atrophy progression in people with MS, providing a mechanistic framework to understand neurodegeneration in MS.

title: Inhibition of aberrant astrocyte activity restores auditory sensorimotor function in zebrafish spen mutants
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Sensorimotor deficits can profoundly affect the life quality of patients with neurological disorders, yet our understanding of central dysfunction at the cellular or circuit level is limited. Using a forward genetic approach to generate loss of auditory function in zebrafish larvae, we identified a recessive mutation in
                    split ends
                    (
                    spen
                    ), which encodes a transcription factor implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders in humans. We found that auditory sensorimotor deficits in
                    spen
                    mutants are associated with chronically elevated calcium levels in hindbrain radial astrocytes. Astrocytes have been previously implicated in the integration of neuronal inputs that alter arousal states and sensorimotor behavior. Inhibition of noradrenergic receptors, which are expressed in astrocytes, lowered calcium levels in mutant radial astrocytes and, notably, restored behavioral responses to sound in
                    spen
                    mutants. Our study highlights a role for noradrenergic signaling in
                    spen
                    -related disease and points to potential therapeutic approaches for pediatric patients.

title: The transcription factors OsIDD and OsSHR jointly regulate ground tissue patterning and differentiation in rice roots
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Rice roots have a distinctive ground tissue architecture with multiple cortical layers and a single endodermal layer concentrically surrounding the stele. This architecture promotes aerenchyma formation and adaptability to waterlogged environments, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here, we identified the INDETERMINATE DOMAIN (IDD) and SHORTROOT (SHR) families as key regulators of ground tissue development in rice. OsIDD2/3/6/8 govern cortical radial symmetry by coordinating cortical organization and auxin distribution independently of OsSHR1/2/3/4/5. Quadruple knockout of
                    OsIDD2/3/6/8
                    caused cortical asymmetry without affecting apoplastic barrier integrity or mineral uptake but reduced shoot-directed ion transport. OsIDD8 also controls the number of cortical cell layers and endodermal cells, whereas OsSHR1/2/3/4/5 redundantly promote periclinal divisions of the cortical cells, which require OsIDD8 activity. Moreover, OsIDD and OsSHR members coordinate endodermal differentiation by regulating localization of Casparian strip membrane domain protein OsCASP1 and lignin/suberin deposition. These findings establish a genetic framework underlying the spatial organization and functional differentiation of ground tissue in rice roots.

title: Chromatin dynamics secondary to dexamethasone exposure identifies 67 genes linked to elevated IOP and primary open-angle glaucoma
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder, and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) represents its only modifiable risk factor. We modeled increased IOP by treating three primary human trabecular meshwork cell strains with dexamethasone and generated a high-resolution map of promoter-centered chromatin contacts and regulatory modules. We identify dynamic changes in chromatin compartments and looping, cis-regulatory elements, and transcription factor hubs corresponding to altered expression profile. By integrating Genomewide association studies associated variants with dexamethasone induced chromatin landscape, we ascertain 29 target genes linked to 23 lead IOP variants and 57 genes for 46 POAG variants, with 19 shared between the two. Pathway analysis of 67 IOP- and POAG-associated genes reveals enrichment in vesicle transport, TLR, MAPK, and hippo-YAP signaling pathways. We also uncover transcriptional regulatory role of 103 noncoding lead variants. Our studies provide a mechanistic framework of genetic complexity accompanying steroid-induced IOP and related POAG pathology.

title: Evolutionarily reinforced GC-rich motif enables non-AUG translation in mammals under eIF1/5MP-mediated fidelity control
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Non-AUG translation contributes to proteome diversity, but its regulatory principles remain unclear. Here, we show that a GCC-rich upstream extension, termed the
                    NAT1
                    motif, acts as a potent enhancer of near-cognate initiation in mammals. Cell-free and reporter assays revealed that eIF1 and 5MP act as conserved inhibitors of non-AUG initiation across mammals and plants, while the
                    NAT1
                    motif enables enhanced initiation within this fidelity framework. Mutational analysis identified −6 and −7 positions within the GCC repeat as key determinants of motif activity. Genome-wide analyses uncovered evolutionary depletion of
                    NAT1
                    -type non-AUG codons in human 5′UTRs, suggesting purifying selection against excessive initiation. Nevertheless, more than a hundred retained sites are associated with genes involved in cell proliferation and migration, suggesting that regulated non-AUG initiation may contribute to disease-relevant translational programs. The motif’s enrichment within GCC repeats further suggests a mechanistic link to repeat-associated non-AUG translation.

title: Linear scaling reveals low-dimensional structure in observable microbial dynamics
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Microbial communities often exhibit apparently complex dynamics driven by myriad interactions among community members and with their environments. Yet, practical modeling and control are often based on a limited number of observables, raising fundamental questions: are these observed dynamics low-dimensional? If so, how does the low dimensionality enable predictions with limited information? Here, we report an emergent simplicity that the temporal dynamics of observable microbial populations can be captured by low-dimensional representations. Using variational autoencoders, we define a critical latent dimension (
                    
                      E
                      c
                    
                    ) that operationally quantifies the smallest latent dimension required for high-fidelity reconstruction of observable microbial dynamics under a specified criterion. Despite the complexity of unobserved background dynamics, we find
                    
                      E
                      c
                    
                    to be drastically lower than the community’s apparent degrees of freedom.
                    
                      E
                      c
                    
                    scales linearly with the number of observables, providing an empirical principle for determining representation complexity. This principle holds across simulations of pairwise interacting communities, consumer–resource dynamics, spatially distributed microbial patches, and plasmid transfer, experiments with engineered and environment-derived communities, and human microbiomes. Our findings establish a scaling law for microbial community dynamics and demonstrate that low-dimensional representations of observable dynamics retain information useful for selected prediction tasks without direct measurement of the complete community.

title: Phosphatases regulating ERK activation and ERK-dependent cell migration
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) have essential roles in development and are implicated in numerous diseases. ERKs are activated by phosphorylation and are regulated by dephosphorylation. To study the ERK phosphatases, we adapted a method to monitor ERK activity in live, unfixed preparations that accommodates the highly dynamic temporal and spatial features of ERK activation. We evaluated 140 human phosphatases using an in vivo reporter (ERK-SPARK) for high-throughput screening in human cells, and we used an in vivo
                    Drosophila
                    model for functional validation of their phosphatase homologs. We found that EYA family phosphatases are critical regulators of ERK signaling both in
                    Drosophila
                    and in mammalian cells and found that inhibition of human EYA4, a homolog of
                    Drosophila
                    Eyes Absent phosphatase, enhances migration of ERK-responsive tumor cells. These findings have important implications for the development of therapeutics.

title: Intermittent Cauchy walks enable optimal 3D search across target shapes and sizes
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Efficiently locating rare targets requires balancing the exploration of novel space with the exploitation of local vicinities. While this tradeoff is well documented in simplified environments, its behavior in realistic three-dimensional environments remains unclear. Here, we analyze intermittent Lévy walks in three dimensions and show that search efficiency becomes strongly dependent on target geometry, with volume, surface area, and elongation governing performance across the Lévy spectrum. Against this geometric complexity, the Cauchy walk (

Our findings provide a theoretical framework for biological movement patterns, including marine predator foraging and immune surveillance, and inform the design of efficient search algorithms for engineered systems such as autonomous nanoscale explorers.

title: Structural insights into the evolution of mitochondrial protein import from the trypanosome ATOM complex
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) mediates the import of most mitochondrial preproteins. In the protozoan parasite
                    Trypanosoma brucei
                    , this machinery is replaced by the atypical translocase of the outer membrane (ATOM), whose composition differs substantially from the canonical TOM complexes of fungi and metazoans. Here, we report the cryoelectron microscopy structure of the
                    T. brucei
                    ATOM complex at 2.8 Å resolution. The structure resolves all previously identified components together with an additional, previously uncharacterized subunit. Despite its divergent composition, ATOM retains a conserved dimeric channel architecture and a protein-conducting pathway closely resembling those of opisthokont TOM complexes, indicating that the core mechanism of mitochondrial protein translocation was established early in eukaryotic evolution. In contrast, the receptor and intermembrane-space regions exhibit distinct architectures, revealing extensive evolutionary diversification and multiple examples of convergent evolution. Together, these findings provide a near-atomic view of the ATOM translocase and offer insights into the origin, conservation, and diversification of the mitochondrial protein import machinery across eukaryotes.

title: Dynamic supercoiling sponsors transcription amplification by MYC
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Dysregulated MYC provokes profound changes in cancer gene expression. Although usually considered an E-box-dependent transcription activator, an alternate model is that MYC is a universal amplifier of transcription. Although MYC participates in pause release, its full role in the transcription cycle remains poorly illuminated. MYC also stimulates topoisomerases to resolve DNA topological issues complicating its transactions; how this stimulation is coordinated with its transcriptional role has not been examined. We have developed a system that discriminates between MYC-driven activation versus amplification in any cell. This system enables the interrogation of genes, cofactors, and compounds that execute or modulate MYC activity. Using a combination of biochemical and cellular assays, we reveal dynamic interplay between MYC-driven transcription amplification and DNA supercoiling. Because the early stages of transcription are sensitive to DNA supercoiling, Reducing TOP1 activity 1 either through genetic knockdown or low-dose inhibition, potentiates transcription amplification by MYC. By increasing promoter melting and RNA polymerase loading, negative supercoiling provides the early transcription complexes upon which MYC acts to increase output.

title: RE1 silencing transcription factor is reduced in endometriosis, and uterine deletion in mice alters progesterone responsiveness
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Endometriosis is a steroid-dependent gynecologic disease characterized by progesterone (P4) resistance, subfertility/infertility, and pelvic pain; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying impaired P4 responsiveness in endometriosis tissue are not fully understood. RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST), a transcriptional regulator implicated in steroid hormone signaling, has emerged as a potential mediator of P4 responsiveness. Here, we investigated the role of REST in endometriosis using human tissues and a uterine-specific Rest conditional knockout mouse model. Immunohistochemical analysis of eutopic endometrium and ectopic lesions from patients with endometriosis revealed significantly reduced nuclear REST expression compared with control endometrium, suggesting loss of functional REST in disease. To assess the physiological consequences of REST deficiency, uterine-specific Rest knockout (Rest
                    d/d
                    ) mice were generated. Rest
                    d/d
                    females exhibited progressive subfertility and hyperestrogenic uterine tissue characteristics that displayed a blunted responsiveness to P4 treatment. Loss of Rest selectively altered expression of P4-responsive genes associated with endometriosis pathology, despite preserved P4 receptor expression. Following induction of experimental endometriosis, female mice that developed endometriotic-like lesions using Rest-deficient donor tissue developed significantly larger lesions that were less responsive to P4 treatment compared to lesions induced using control tissue. Mechanical sensitivity was modestly increased in mice receiving Rest-deficient tissue, whereas vaginal hyperalgesia was unaffected. These findings identify loss of nuclear REST as a feature of endometriosis and support a role of REST in subfertility, lesion progression, and blunted response to P4. REST may represent a molecular contributor to altered P4 responsiveness and a potential therapeutic target in endometriosis.

title: PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 moderates the activity of phytochrome A in persistent canopy shade conditions
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: In nature, plants perceive and respond to complex vegetative environments through the phytochrome (phy) photoreceptor-signaling system. The Canopy Adaptation Strategy, elicited by phyA, together with the Shade Avoidance Syndrome, regulated by phyB, enables plants to adapt to diverse forms of vegetation shade. The phyA High Irradiance Response mode, which involves photocycle-coupled nuclear shuttling, is essential for sensing sustained far-red-rich conditions typical of canopy or occlusive shade. Our research identifies PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 (PIF7) as a key regulator of phyA function. We show that PIF7 overexpression (PIF7ox) effectively suppresses phyA action. Under persistent shade, PIF7 and phyA both accumulate and associate within nuclear photobodies, with this interaction mediated by the C-terminal domain of PIF7 and the PAS-PAS domain of phyA. PIF7 also interacts with FAR-RED ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 1 (FHY1) and FHY1-LIKE transport facilitators, thereby interfering with phyA cytosolic-nuclear shuttling. This coordinated molecular targeting by PIF7 constitutes an effective strategy for modulating phyA function under persistent shade conditions.

title: Recurrent hybridization between highly divergent paramecium species
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The process of speciation, through which two reproductively isolated species emerge from an ancestral population, is often gradual, including a period during which gene flow still occurs, and hence speciation remains reversible. However, if isolation persists, the progressive accumulation of genetic incompatibilities ultimately locks the speciation process, reaching the point where hybrid offspring are inviable or sterile. In plants and animals, the establishment of species barriers is quite rapid: Beyond a net genetic divergence of 0.02 substitutions per synonymous site, interspecific introgressions become extremely rare. Here we report that in ciliates, species barriers can be broken despite huge genetic divergence. We show that the genome of
                    Paramecium sonneborni
                    contains hundreds of DNA segments that were acquired by recurrent horizontal transfers from multiple very distant lineages (synonymous divergence ~1 substitution/site). These segments approach the size of full-length chromosomes, which indicates that they were introgressed by interspecific mating. These data show that in the ancestry of
                    P. sonneborni
                    , hybridization events with highly divergent species occurred repeatedly and led to viable and fertile offspring. We propose that this unexpected promiscuous sexual behavior is made possible by the fact that paramecia separate somatic and germline functions in two types of nuclei: The elimination of non-self-DNA fragments during the development of the somatic genome allows individuals of a species to remain phenotypically the same, despite recurrent genetic flow from distant species into their germline.
