title: Lipid droplets buffer hydrogen sulfide–induced redox imbalance
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The electron transport chain is a signaling hub for hydrogen sulfide (H
                    2
                    S) that serves both as a respiratory substrate and an inhibitor. While acute sulfide toxicity is well characterized, cellular adaptations to chronic H
                    2
                    S, particularly microbially-derived sulfide exposure in colon, is poorly understood. We report that chronic, low-level H
                    2
                    S exposure (4 to 20 µM) drives robust carbon sequestration in lipid droplets (LD) across several human cell lines, driven by a coordinated remodeling of redox and nucleotide metabolism. Specifically, H
                    2
                    S-induced reductive shifts in nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and coenzyme Q (CoQ) pools are accompanied by glycerol-3-phosphate accumulation and cytidine triphosphate (CTP) depletion. Lipidomic analysis reveals increased neutral lipid synthesis and triacylglyceride accumulation concomitant with decreased CTP-dependent synthesis of membrane phospholipids. Mitochondrial expression of a water-generating NADH oxidase attenuates LD accumulation and spatially confines the origin of H
                    2
                    S-induced reductive stress signaling to this compartment. Interestingly, LD abundance increases even after H
                    2
                    S withdrawal, continuing over 48 h, during which time the reductively-shifted NAD and CoQ pools slowly reoxidize. Inhibition of fatty acid synthesis during sulfide exposure impairs cellular recovery of respiration. These findings establish an active role for LDs in stress response and reveal that lipid biogenesis is a strategy for countering H
                    2
                    S-induced redox imbalance. The sulfide–LD–redox axis uncovered in this study has implications for understanding how gut-derived H
                    2
                    S, shaped by diet and microbiome, can influence metabolic health.

title: Modest loss of sleep increases susceptibility to cybersecurity threats
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Sleep restriction leads to impaired cognitive processing across domains. I examined whether the transition to daylight saving time (DST), typically accompanied by compromised sleep, would lead to an increase in the probability of falling prey to a simulated phishing attack using a fully naturalistic experiment with random assignment and blinding. A predatory email was sent to employees at the University of California, Irvine (N = 11,218) either on the morning of Monday following the transition to DST or one week earlier. The transition led to a ~13% increase in the probability of clicking a suspicious link, without affecting the probability of opening the email or reporting it as spam. These results demonstrate that even modest, mundane, and acute loss of sleep has real-life, potentially hazardous, implications for cognitive function.

title: Neuromelanin-inspired metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks restore neuronal excitability in radiation-induced brain injury
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) affects up to 30% of patients receiving cranial radiotherapy, representing an irreversible complication lacking effective therapies. Research advances are limited by poor blood-brain barrier drug penetration and overreliance on ex vivo pathology, which cannot resolve dynamic neuronal dysfunction. Inspired by neuromelanin, we fabricated metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks (MSMNs), combined with in vivo electrophysiology to investigate and mitigate radiation-triggered neural dysfunction. In 6-gray whole body–irradiated mice, MSMN normalized neuronal excitability and restored medium spiny neuron firing and striatal circuit activity, improving locomotor and anxiety-related behaviors. Besides central functional recovery, MSMN provides systemic radioprotection, ensuring full 30-day survival, protecting radiosensitive organs and facilitating hematopoietic recovery. This work identifies neuronal excitability as an underexplored therapeutic target for RIBI, establishing neuromelanin-mimetic selenomelanin nanonetworks as a bioinspired platform linking molecular radioprotection to circuit-level restoration for radiation-induced neurological injury.

title: PPP1R1B differentially modulates alcohol intake and emotional comorbidity through distinct prefrontal circuits
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Excessive alcohol consumption frequently co-occurs with anxiety and depression in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms coordinating these comorbid conditions remain poorly defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly its prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions, projects to key reward and emotion centers like the nucleus accumbens (Nac) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but the functional heterogeneity of these projections is unclear. Using chemogenetics, retrograde tracing, electrophysiology, spatial proteomics, and cell-type-specific gene editing in mice subjected to a 4-wk intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) paradigm, we selectively manipulated glutamatergic projections from the PL and IL to the Nac core, Nac shell, and BLA and assessed alcohol intake, anxiety-like, and depression-like behaviors. Chemogenetic activation of PL-Nac core projections reduced short-term alcohol intake, anxiety-, and depression-like behaviors, while IL-BLA activation decreased alcohol consumption and anxiety-like behaviors only. Retrograde tracing revealed mirror-image anatomical segregation of projection-defined neuronal subpopulations within PL/IL linking spatial organization to functional divergence. IAA induced pathway-specific synaptic adaptations. Spatial proteomics nominated protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a candidate molecule in PL-Nac core neurons. Independent immunostaining confirmed PPP1R1B downregulation, and circuit-specific knockout recapitulated alcohol-related and affective phenotypes, whereas overexpression reversed them. In IL-BLA neurons, PPP1R1B manipulation modulated alcohol intake and anxiety, but not depression. These findings define a subregion- and projection-specific organizational logic in the mPFC for differentially regulating alcohol consumption and emotional comorbidity, with PPP1R1B as a key molecular determinant. This provides a neural pathway–molecule framework for targeted intervention in AUD.

title: Wearable interstitial fluid sensing of time-resolved uric acid for early prediction of flare-associated pain in an induced mouse model
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Gout flare is driven by hyperuricemia (HUA) and inflammatory responses to monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, yet single time-point serum uric acid (UA) measurements cannot capture the biochemical dynamics preceding flare onset or explain the timing of severe pain manifestation. Here, we present a skin-attachable interstitial fluid (ISF)-based electrochemical sensing platform for time-resolved, minimally invasive UA monitoring in a controlled, induced mouse model of gout flare-associated inflammation and pain. The platform integrates an enzyme-based UA sensor, a thin insertion electrode, and battery-free near-field communication (NFC), enabling time-resolved in vivo tracking of ISF UA dynamics. By establishing disease-stage-specific models comprising HUA, MSU-only inflammation, and gouty arthritis flare (GA flare) conditions, we separately examined metabolic and inflammatory contributions to flare-associated UA dynamics. Time-resolved ISF monitoring revealed that the GA flare group exhibited pronounced UA fluctuation patterns that were not reproduced by either condition alone. The peak timing of UA dynamics was temporally decoupled from pain-related behavioral responses, indicating that flare-associated pain onset cannot be explained by a single UA concentration. A machine learning framework using ISF UA time-series features identified predictive information preceding peak pain, whereas analyses using earlier events defined by sustained decreases in paw withdrawal threshold showed lower and event-definition-dependent performance. These findings establish time-resolved ISF UA monitoring as a framework for resolving flare-associated biochemical dynamics and evaluating subsequent pain progression in an induced mouse model.

title: Physiologic and pharmacologic role of the glucocorticoid receptor in germinal center B cells and plasmacytic differentiation
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
In diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a malignancy derived from germinal center (GC) B cells, somatic hypermutation aberrantly targets glucocorticoid receptor (GR) binding sequences in the super-enhancer (SE) of multiple oncogenes. These events abrogate GR binding and deregulate the expression of the SE-linked gene, suggesting an important role of GR in normal and transformed GC B cells. Using a GC-specific
                    Nr3c1
                    knockout mouse model and multi-omics analyses in murine and human GC B cells, here we show that, under physiological conditions, GR constitutively localizes to the nucleus, where it transcriptionally modulates signaling pathways implicated in GC homeostasis and plasmablast differentiation in part by antagonizing the repressive function of BCL6 on the plasma cell master regulators IRF4 and PRDM1. While loss of baseline GR activity led to mild GC hyperplasia and impaired plasmacytic differentiation, pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoids, a key component of DLBCL chemo-immunotherapy, were preferentially toxic to GC in a GC B cell–autonomous manner. These findings uncover a physiological role for GR in the GC reaction as well as in promoting plasmablast/plasma cell formation and provide insights into the specific activity of glucocorticoids in the treatment of DLBCL.

title: Dormancy stabilizes structured food webs
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Theory predicts that strong species interactions drive instability in large ecosystems, but strong interactions are common in nature while strong instability appears rare. This discrepancy motivates enduring interest in ecological mechanisms that limit or counteract instability. Dormancy—reversible metabolic suppression—may be one. Dormancy is a ubiquitous life history trait found in organisms ranging from bacteria to trees. Dormant individuals form “seed banks” that are temporarily disengaged from demographic processes and species interactions, creating a memory of past ecological dynamics. Seed banks can stabilize predator–prey interactions, but whether, when, and how they affect the stability of larger ecological networks is uncertain. We show that dormancy stabilizes oscillatory dynamics in a minimal mathematical model and illustrate how dormancy converts high oscillation frequency into strong restoring force. We find that dormancy can have qualitative stabilizing effects in structured food webs that undergo Hopf bifurcations and exhibit oscillatory instability, but rarely in unstructured networks or networks with symmetric (competitive or mutualistic) interactions. This classification remains accurate when only some species go dormant and drive stabilization. Our results clarify when dormancy can promote stability, indicating that it may be an important but overlooked stabilizing factor in food webs.

title: Phylogenetic profiling reveals evolutionary coupling between methyltransferases and the cytoskeleton
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Methylation is a fundamental post-translational modification best understood as regulating chromatin structure and gene expression, yet there is emerging evidence that methylation also shapes cytoskeletal organization, regulating key processes such as mitosis and cell migration. Proteomic studies have revealed cytoskeletal protein methylation is widespread, however little is known about the enzymes responsible for these modifications, or their evolutionary relationship to other, better known substrates for methylation, such as chromatin. To address this question, we applied phylogenetic profiling across the complete repertoire of human methyltransferases to identify conserved functional relationships extending beyond chromatin. Unbiased clustering revealed extensive coevolution between methyltransferases and many components of the cytoskeleton, uncovering a previously unrecognized evolutionary network linking canonical chromatin regulatory enzymes to cellular structural systems. Evolutionary Trace analysis of the H3K36 methyltransferase family recovered known catalytic and regulatory domains while identifying additional evolutionarily constrained residues, suggesting previously unappreciated functional interfaces. Comparative analyses further distinguished deeply conserved methyltransferase–cytoskeletal relationships from those that emerged later during eukaryotic evolution, indicating that cytoskeletal methylation comprises both ancient and lineage-expanded regulatory programs. Leveraging these evolutionary signatures, we identified and experimentally validated a previously unrecognized association between the methyltransferase NSD3 and α-tubulin. Together, these findings reveal that methyltransferases traditionally viewed as chromatin regulators participate in an evolutionarily conserved network that coordinates nuclear and cytoskeletal functions. More broadly, they establish phylogenetic profiling as a powerful approach for discovering noncanonical activities of chromatin-associated enzymes and suggest that regulation of chromatin organization and cellular architecture evolved as interconnected processes.

title: Multi-omics characterization of white matter free water reveals genetic and vascular determinants of neurological disorders
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: White matter free water (FW-WM), quantified using diffusion MRI, reflects extracellular water content and microstructural alterations within water matter, but its genetic architecture and clinical relevance remain largely uncharted. We conducted a multi-omics study integrating 42,039 individuals from the UK Biobank and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohorts to characterize tract-specific FW-WM across genetic, phenotypic, and proteomic dimensions. Genome-wide association analyses identified 27 independent loci and prioritized 88 genes, which were enriched in the genomic functional elements of vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytes. Notably, 20 loci (74%) were novel compared to conventional white matter metrics. Both genetic predisposition to higher FW-WM and imaging-derived FW-WM were associated with a spectrum of neurological disorders. Specifically, imaging-derived FW-WM showed strong associations with stroke (OR = 3.14) and dementia (OR = 4.15), while higher baseline FW-WM predicted progression from MCI to AD (HR = 2.58). Bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses further supported genetically predicted associations between hypertension and FW-WM, which were together associated with increased risks of stroke and cognitive impairment. Integrative proteomic analyses further nominated PEAR1 and ANGL3 as candidate proteins potentially linking hypertension-related vascular processes to FW-WM variation. Together, these findings provide a multi-omics characterization of FW-WM that connects genetic susceptibility, vascular factors, and neurological outcomes, supporting FW-WM as a tract-specific imaging phenotype with potential utility for neurological risk stratification.

title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub–grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert–vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub–grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity science with ecology, offering a pathway toward bottom-up ecosystem understanding.

title: Superoxide dismutase shapes manganese stoichiometry in Southern Ocean diatoms
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Quantifying the elemental stoichiometry of marine phytoplankton biomass is crucial for projections of primary production. In many cases, the mechanistic underpinnings of biomass stoichiometry are unclear. We combined metaproteomics, Bayesian statistical modeling, and geochemical measurements to quantify the contribution of superoxide dismutases to metal stoichiometry in natural populations of Southern Ocean diatoms. Our analyses indicate that a substantial amount of manganese (Mn) in diatoms in an Antarctic polynya can be attributed to superoxide dismutases (∼0.7 micromoles of Mn:moles of carbon; ∼20% of the total cellular Mn quota). We then used proteomic profiles of polar diatom cultures to identify environmental controls on superoxide dismutases and found that Mn limitation induces the depletion of Mn superoxide dismutases and an accompanying increase in nickel superoxide dismutase. Overall, we combined metaproteomic approaches to quantify proteome composition and connected these measurements to metal-to-carbon ratios and their responses to metal availability. Our approach provides a mechanism for directly parameterizing ecosystem-scale models with molecular measurements.

title: Passive imaging with quantum advantage
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Far-field optical imaging inevitably involves low-pass spatial filtering, limiting the resolution. Moreover, conventional imaging suppresses high spatial frequency components close to the cutoff, making them invisible under noise—particularly the shot noise arising from discrete and random nature of quantum light. Here, we propose and implement a method for reducing the effect of this noise by optically preprocessing the incoming light before detection, thereby optimizing the quantum measurement performed on it. Our scheme, termed Fourier domain division (FDD), partitions the Fourier plane into multiple regions for independent detection and subsequent post-processing for image reconstruction. By analyzing the quantum and classical Fisher information, we show that our method is advantageous with respect to direct imaging for high spatial-frequency components. As a result, the number of photons required to achieve a certain signal-to-noise ratio in the Fourier domain is reduced, thus enhancing the overall resolution in the photon-starved regime. We demonstrate our method in microscopy, achieving fivefold improvement of Fisher information on high spatial frequency components. Unlike active super-resolution methods, FDD is passive, making it broadly applicable in microscopy and other imaging scenarios, where active illumination is impractical, including astronomy and remote sensing, in the photon-starved regime. Our work establishes a general strategy for designing quantum optimized superresolution imaging systems, bridging fundamental quantum limits, practical image analysis, and computer vision applications.

title: A primordial heavy water reservoir in the outer solar system
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The oxygen (O) isotopic composition of outer solar system ices is believed to be enriched in heavy O isotopes owing to photochemical processes, but evidence for this O reservoir is exceedingly rare in meteorites. Hydrated interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) collected in Earth’s stratosphere that display high densities of solar energetic particle tracks originate from Edgeworth-Kuiper belt objects. Their mineralogy is dominated by hydrated minerals that formed by alteration of anhydrous precursor minerals at low temperatures through reactions with water (H
                    2
                    O)–carbon dioxide fluids. The O isotopic compositions of track-rich hydrated IDPs implicate
                    17,18
                    O-rich ices as the source of H
                    2
                    O involved in their alteration, providing compelling evidence for the presence of a major heavy water reservoir beyond the orbits of the gas giant planets that was largely isolated from inner solar system materials.

title: Dynamic plasmonic imaging of electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for charge-resolved multiplex biosensing
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Multiplexed profiling of diverse biomarkers is essential for precision diagnostics, but remains challenging for label-free sensors because signals typically scale with analyte mass. Here, we present a dynamic plasmonic imaging platform based on electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for multiplexed, label-free quantification of nucleic acids, proteins, and small molecules within a unified sensing architecture. Size-encoded nanoparticles tethered to a plasmonic surface are electrically actuated to oscillate vertically within the evanescent field and tracked by distance-resolved surface plasmon resonance imaging. Molecular binding alters the effective surface charge of each nano-oscillator, modulating the electrostatic-driven forces and changing oscillation amplitude. This charge-to-motion transduction mechanism reduces dependence on molecular mass and enhances sensitivity for low–molecular weight analytes. This platform simultaneously detects microRNAs, proteins, and small molecules spanning a ∼300-fold molecular weight range within a single field of view. We further demonstrate multiplexed profiling of tumor-associated microRNAs in pretreated supernatants from patient-derived breast cancer cells across 24 clinical samples. Dynamic plasmonic nano-oscillators provide a scalable architecture for multiplex molecular diagnostics.

title: Integrating biomass production platform and identification approach for stereochemical assignment of super-carbon-chain compounds
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Super-carbon-chain compounds (SCCCs), marine long-carbon-chain polyketides featuring numerous carbon stereocenters, fall into untapped chemical space in between drug-like small molecules and biopolymers. Due to mass-material unavailability and flexible-structure complexity, the reliable stereochemical assignment of SCCCs has long remained stagnant. In this work, a modern microalgal biomass production-platform is created for pilot-scale cultivation of marine dinoflagellates to produce over 100 milligrams of minor SCCCs. The modular fragment-based identification (MFBI) approach is successfully employed to establish the relative and absolute configurations of SCCCs. As an example, 157.7 mg of a minor SCCC, named amphidiketol A, featuring a highly-flexible C
                    76
                    -linear carbon backbone and thirty-three carbon stereocenters, is obtained from
                    Amphidinium
                    sp. in our platform. Its hybrid architecture contains eleven‌ distinct modular fragments. Its relative and absolute configurations are successfully established by the MFBI approach. Collectively, an undescribed paradigm for stereochemical assignment of SCCCs is presented. Nine senescence-associated protein targets of amphidiketol A in lung cancer A549 cells are identified.

title: STAT3 controls IL-6–induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pleiotropic cytokine that drives macrophage functions ranging from tissue homeostasis to inflammation, yet how STAT3 specifies these divergent outcomes remains unclear. By integrating transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with selective STAT3 degradation, we show that STAT3 controls IL-6–induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages. Graded STAT3 chromatin recruitment scales with locus-specific H3K27ac deposition and transcriptional output across homeostatic and inflammatory programs. STAT3 degradation permits STAT1 recruitment at a subset of regulatory regions and engages a delayed amplification loop that is partially dependent on STING and type I IFN signaling. In severe COVID-19, monocytes exhibit exaggerated STAT3-associated inflammatory signatures together with attenuated STAT1-associated interferon responses, consistent with a skewed STAT3-STAT1 balance. These findings define a framework in which STAT3 calibrates IL-6–induced chromatin output while maintaining pathway fidelity by limiting STAT1 cross-talk.

title: Principles of use of tensile J-curve materials in antagonistic arrangements
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Natural ligaments are soft connective tissues that provide high stretchability for dexterous flexibility but switch to high stiffness to protect the musculoskeletal system from excessive deformation. These two functions cannot be independently tuned in conventional engineering materials with linear or hyperelasticity. Biological materials achieve this tailored behavior through a highly nonlinear tensile response characterized by a J-shaped curve, featuring an extended “toe region” of low force up to intermediate strains followed by an inflection, called the “heel region” which marks the onset of nonlinear stiffening. Here, we aim to study the characteristics of J-curves to establish principles for their use in robotic mechanisms. We define and measure the J-curve features responsible for protectiveness and mobility, describe the effective stiffness and the level of nonlinearity as a function of pre-stretch, and elucidate how the J-curve decouples flexibility from damage protection. Experimental measurements reveal the performance advantages of twisted and coiled elastomeric J-curve materials in engineered antagonistic arrangements and highlight their unique design space compared with linear elastic systems. Furthermore, we present a conceptual analysis of exploiting J-curve materials in energy-efficient running as an outlook toward their use in bioinspired robots.

title: Lewis Acid‐Activated High‐Entropy Layered Double Hydroxide for Superior Seawater Electrolysis
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Seawater electrolysis has been identified as a sustainable approach for the industrialization of green hydrogen. However, this process is hindered by two significant factors: the sluggish anodic kinetics and chloride‐induced corrosion. In this study, we introduce Zn 2+ as a Lewis acid site into high‐entropy layered double hydroxide (LDH) to modulate both the interfacial microenvironment and the bulk electronic structure. The resulting catalyst requires overpotentials of 35 and 160 mV for the hydrogen/oxygen evolution reactions at 10 mA cm −2 , respectively, accompanied by small Tafel slopes. Furthermore, an anion‐exchange membrane electrolyzer demonstrates operational stability over a duration of 900 h at 1.5 A cm −2 . Theoretical and in situ analyses reveal that Zn 2+ exhibits a preference for adsorbing OH − , thereby repelling Cl − . Concurrently, this process induces oxygen vacancies and optimizes the d‑band centers of Fe/Co sites, establishing a interfacial/bulk dual regulation. This work offers a novel paradigm for the design of robust high‑entropy catalysts via Lewis acid doping for practical applications in harsh environments.

title: Bioinspired Buffered Microenvironment Enables Highly Crystalline 3D COF Gels With Controllable Structures for Exceptional Molecular Adsorption
source: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Reconciling long‐range crystallinity with macroscopic network formation remains a central challenge in constructing three‐dimensional covalent organic framework (3D COF) gels. Inspired by biomineralization and tofu coagulation, we propose a synergistic buffered system with salt bridges for direct assembly of crystalline 3D COF gels via imine condensation. Ten metal salts were selected to regulate stable and buffered pH microenvironment. Comparing various salts revealed a correlation between pH microenvironment and the formation state and crystallinity of COFs. NaAc emerges as representative regulator for multiple roles: (i) forming AcO − /AcOH buffer to maintain a stable weakly acidic microenvironment and promote disorder‐to‐order transition, (ii) regulating kinetics, defect healing, and COF topology, and (iii) Na + as salt bridges stabilizing the 3D gel network. Pore topology can be switched between two crystalline phases by varying side substituents and salt addition sequence, as seen by XRD peak shift from 8.9° to 6.6°. The gels have low density (0.028–0.042 g/cm 3 ), high compressive strength, CO 2 /N 2 selectivity of 140, organic solvent uptake up to 80 times their weight, and over 90% capacity retention after 20 cycles. Overall, this work establishes a paradigm from microenvironment engineering and ion selection to topology regulation and adsorption, providing a blueprint for functional 3D COF gels.

Cu-Doped Highly Porous SnO2 for Long-Lasting Acidic CO2 Electroreduction at 1000 mA cm–2
abstract: Abstract Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to formic acid (HCOOH) provides a carbon-neutral route. SnO2-based catalysts suffer from limited activity and instability at industrial current densities. We develop a Cu-doped highly porous SnO2 catalyst (SnO2-Cu) that enhances activity and stabilizes the SnO2 framework. The porous structure exposes numerous active sites while confining local OH– within the bulk acid electrolyte, enabling high-current-density operation. Cu doping strengthens CO2 chemisorption and Sn–O bond covalency, boosting CO2RR activity while suppressing SnO2 self-reduction. SnO2-Cu sustains 1000 mA cm–2 for 19 h with 98.5% FE and 800 mA cm–2 for 72 h with 94.1% FE in a flow cell at pH 1.82. It achieves a HCOOH production cost of 722.7 USD tonne–1 in a solid-state electrolyte (SSE) device calculated based on onshore wind power, demonstrating economic competitiveness. This work demonstrates that rational Cu doping of porous SnO2 addresses activity and durability limits, offering an effective platform for high-rate, economically viable HCOOH electrosynthesis.

title: Regulation of Anionic Redox Reaction Voltage by Energy Band Modulation for Li-Rich Cathodes
abstract: Abstract Anionic redox reaction (ARR) promises high energy density for Li-rich cathodes yet suffers from severe voltage decay. Here, we investigate ARR voltage modulation in a Li2S-modified quasi-solid Li-rich cathode (Li2S-LRM), which exhibits a distinct low-voltage ARR plateau (2.0–2.8 V). Combining in situ XRD, S K-edge XANES, EELS, Ar-etched XPS and DFT calculations, we validate in situ electrochemical sulfur doping. Upon cycling, the material forms bulk LixS/Li–S–O species alongside a dominant Li2SO3/Li2SO4 polyanion interphase that realizes oxygen trapping. Vacancy-cluster formation facilitates reversible S-involved charge compensation, where sulfur redox activity progressively intensifies during long cycling. Enabled by the band-modulation and oxygen-trapping effects, Li2S-LRM achieves a high average Coulombic efficiency of 99.6% and suppressed voltage decay (0.28 vs. 0.83 mV cycle–1 for pristine LRM). This work deepens mechanistic insights into ARR and provides rational design guidance for high-performance anionic-redox cathodes.

title: Spatiotemporal Molecular Control of Crystallization for Efficient Perovskite/Organic Tandem Photovoltaics
abstract: Abstract Perovskite/organic tandem solar cells (PO-TSCs) offer a route toward overcoming the efficiency limitations of single-junction photovoltaics. However, wide-bandgap (WBG) perovskite sub-cells limit their performance, where uncontrolled crystallization leads to compositional heterogeneity, defect accumulation, and severe halide phase segregation. Here, we develop a template-bridge dual-control (TBDC) strategy using 2-thiophenemethylammonium bromide (2-ThMAB). Precisely controlling the introduction timing and spatial distribution of 2-ThMAB maximizes molecular regulation of crystallization. Surface-anchored 2-ThMAB molecules act as growth templates to induce (100) crystal growth, while grain-boundary-localized molecules regulate halide migration through molecular bridging, enabling homogeneous crystallization. The WBG perovskite films exhibit enhanced out-of-plane (100) orientation, reduced defect density, and suppressed halide phase segregation. Consequently, the optimized WBG device achieves a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.13% with improved operational stability. Integrated into PO-TSCs, the optimized WBG sub-cells deliver a PCE of 26.62%. This strategy enables concurrent control of crystallization and halide redistribution of efficient, stable tandem photovoltaics.

title: Non-ionic Phthalocyanine Additives Enable Synergistic Passivation and Strain Buffering in Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
abstract: Abstract The long-term stability of high-efficiency n-i-p perovskite solar cells is limited by coupled defect migration, residual lattice strain, and thermal–mechanical degradation. Here, we develop a non-ionic, interface-enriched zinc phthalocyanine derivative, 4PCSZnPc, as a molecular stabilizer for simultaneous defect anchoring and strain buffering. Unlike ionic additives that may introduce mobile species, 4PCSZnPc is distributed throughout the film, with enrichment near the buried SnO2/perovskite interface. Peripheral N/O/S heteroatoms coordinate with under-coordinated Pb2+ sites, while the Zn-regulated macrocyclic center interacts with iodide-related defects, forming dual-site Lewis acid–base anchoring. Meanwhile, the rigid phthalocyanine framework reduces residual tensile stress and may hinder strain-assisted ion migration. These combined effects of defect passivation and strain buffering reduce non-radiative recombination, improve film uniformity, and enhance thermal robustness. Consequently, 4PCSZnPc-treated devices achieve a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.88% (certified 26.74%), a T80 lifetime of 1358 h under 1-sun at 85 °C, and 95% retention after 200 thermal cycles, providing a design principle for future thermally resilient photovoltaics.

title: Engineering Ultrathin, Tough Polymer Networks for Stable Lithium Metal Anode Interphases
abstract: Abstract Interfacial degradation and dendritic lithium (Li) growth remain critical bottlenecks for practical Li metal batteries (LMBs). Herein, we introduce a tough, ion-conductive poly(2-(dimethylamino)ethyl methacrylate) (pDMAEMA) nanolayer on Li metal via photo-initiated chemical vapor deposition (piCVD). The photo-mediated, solvent-free piCVD enables nanometer-scale coatings with systematic control over photo-crosslinking and chain entanglement without compromising Li surface integrity. This systematic control yields an optimized polymer network balancing toughness (36.3 MJ m–3) and viscoelasticity (10.3% linear viscoelastic strain limit) to accommodate repeated Li volume changes. Furthermore, interactions between pDMAEMA and PF6– anions promote a mechanically durable LiF-rich solid electrolyte interphase, thereby supporting uniform Li deposition. Pouch-type bi-cells employing the optimized 100 nm polymer-coated Li anode achieve an energy density of 338 Wh kg–1 and 80% capacity retention after 90 cycles under practical conditions (N/P = 2, E/C = 3 g Ah–1). This ultrathin, tough polymer network offers a promising design principle for high-energy LMBs.

title: Simultaneous Selective Recognition of Two Different Anions within a Hydrogen/Halogen-Bonding Cage
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The search for selective anion receptors that can function in water is a longstanding challenge in supramolecular chemistry, motivated by anions’ fundamental roles (and potential applications) in biological, environmental, and industrial processes. Here, we incorporate halogen and hydrogen bond donors into an easy-to-prepare organic cage molecule and demonstrate that this can bind anions at either or both of a halogen-bonding pocket and hydrogen-bonding pockets depending on the nature of the anions and the solvent. The halogen-bonding pocket comprising six bromopyridinium donors is a potent host for iodide anions and can selectively bind this guest in water as strongly as biological iodide binders (Ka = 43,000 M–1 measured by 1H NMR spectroscopy) with the exclusion of other halide anions. In DMSO/water mixtures, the hydrogen-bonding pockets are able to recognize chloride anions, resulting in the formation of mixed anion iodide/chloride complexes with an iodide bound in the center of the cage and chlorides in the peripheral binding sites. This demonstrates the exquisite selectivity afforded by halogen-bonding systems and reveals a general route to a range of supramolecular anion hosts that bind multiple guests in different locations.

title: Control of Charge Carrier Dynamics and Bandgap Renormalization in CdS Quantum Dot Hybrids by Interface Polarity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Charge carrier dynamics in wurtzite CdS quantum dots (QDs) form the basis for applications in optoelectronics and photocatalysis. We demonstrate that the quantum dynamics, energy gaps, and energy level alignments at CdS QD interfaces can be controlled by the polarity of the CdS QD surface. By performing nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations within a density-functional tight-binding framework, we demonstrate a strong dependence of photoinitiated processes in CdS QDs/graphene nanoribbon (GNR) hybrids on interface polarity. At room temperature, hole transfer is accelerated by a factor of 2 and exciton lifetime is enhanced by nearly an order of magnitude when the CdS QD surface is switched from polar to nonpolar. Remarkably, the interfacial bandgap for the polar QD/GNR hybrid is reduced to half upon heating from 0 K to room temperature, while it remains nearly unchanged for the nonpolar hybrid. At an intermediate temperature, the ultrafast charge separation is maintained; however, charge recombination shows the opposite trend relative to room temperature. The polar interface exhibits a longer lifetime than the nonpolar interface, due to weakened electron–phonon Fröhlich interaction and decreased gap renormalization. The strong and highly nonlinear dependence of bandgap renormalization and carrier dynamics on temperature in the polar QD/GNR hybrid is associated with significant structural reconstruction, which is absent in the nonpolar counterpart. The demonstrated control of excited-state processes by interface polarity and the strong dependence of the dynamics and energy level alignment on temperature provide key fundamental insights for informed design of modern materials for optoelectronics and energy conversion.

title: Breaking the “Micro-Size Inversion” Paradox via a Surface-Chemistry-Driven Molecular Sieving Membrane for Ambient Lithium–Air Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Lithium–air batteries suffer from moisture-induced parasitic reactions and electrolyte evaporation in ambient air. A fundamental challenge is the “micro-size inversion” paradox, where H2O (0.275 nm) is smaller than O2 (0.346 nm), rendering conventional size-based sieving ineffective. Here, we report a composite membrane composed of polydimethylsiloxane and fluorinated vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-VF) to break this selectivity barrier. By grafting 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyl groups onto a vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-V), we establish a surface-chemistry-driven sieving mechanism. This design creates a molecular-level hydrogen-bond-repellent barrier that specifically inhibits polar H2O penetration while maintaining high nonpolar O2 flux, effectively decoupling the permeability-hydrophobicity trade-off. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborate this mechanism, demonstrating that the COF-VF exhibits significantly reduced adsorption affinity toward H2O compared to the pristine COF-V. In 40% RH ambient air, the battery equipped with this membrane delivers a discharge capacity of 3596 mAh g–1 and sustains cycling for 2700 h (270 cycles), a 10.8-fold improvement over unprotected cells. Advanced characterizations via DRT and DEMS confirm that the membrane promotes reversible Li2O2 formation and significantly suppresses LiOH accumulation. This work provides a multiscale strategy for molecular-level selective separation in practical energy storage.

title: Low-Temperature-Mediated Lamellar–Micelle Assembly of Wrinkled Mesoporous Carbon Nanospheres with Aligned Pores and High Interconnectivity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Mesoporous structures with highly permeable channels are of great significance for fast diffusion; however, the delicate engineering of straightforward pores remains quite limited, with most of mesostructures are tortuous pores derived from spherical micelle assembly. Herein, we explore a novel lamellar–micelle assembly approach that enables to generate a type of wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres with highly interconnected divergent mesopores. In place of the conventional spherical micelles, the key for controlling such unusual assembly is determined by the construction of laminar micelles (copolymer L121/F127 composite) and heterogeneous growth on sedimented F127 seeds at a low temperature of 5 °C. The fabricated wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres after template removal possess a particle size at ∼910 nm, a high surface area of 315 m2 g–1, a uniform pore size at 36 nm, as well as radial mesochannels with high interconnectivity up to 96%. Further regulation on the reaction temperature and template ratio allows for a high tunability over the pore size and wrinkle degree. When employed as a sodium storage anode, the radially aligned large-pore structure drastically facilitates charge transport and electrolyte penetration, thus delivering rate capability (142 mAh g–1 at 10 A g–1) and long-term cyclability (90.5% retention after 1000 cycles at 2 A g–1) compared to commercial hard carbon. Our work underscores a particular assembly pathway through lamellar micelles as an effective approach for building up ultrafast mesopore highways toward promising diffusion-related applications.

title: Specific Amino Acid Imaging of Protein Condensates in Live Cells by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Intracellular protein condensates formed by liquid–liquid phase separation have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their key roles in many physiological and pathological processes. However, fluorescence imaging of protein condensates is limited by the bulky fluorescent tags that could perturb the protein localization and interaction. Imaging techniques that can visualize protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbations remain lacking. Here, we develop a strategy to image intracellular protein condensates by coupling stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy to specific amino acid labeling. Different types of amino acids are found to exhibit distinct incorporation patterns in the live cells. By metabolic labeling of deuterated tyrosine-d4 and arginine-d7, ALS-related fused in sarcoma (FUS) protein condensates can be visualized with a high specificity. In addition, two-color pulse-chase imaging reveals protein translation arrest in FUS condensates under stress conditions. Furthermore, heterogeneous tyrosine phosphorylation is imaged in live cells and FUS condensates based on the Raman blue shift of phosphorylated tyrosine-d4. Thus, our technique to image specific amino acids by SRS provides a new platform to visualize the metabolic turnover and post-translational modifications of protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbation.

title: Visible-Light-Driven Dearomatization via Electrocyclic Ring Expansion for Solar Energy Storage
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage compounds capture solar photon energy in the strained chemical bonds of metastable photoisomers and release it on demand as heat, yet simultaneously achieving visible-light absorption and high energy storage density has remained a persistent challenge. Here we introduce 9-aryl acridine N-oxides as MOST compounds based on visible-light-driven dearomative ring expansion. Irradiation at 470 nm, near the solar irradiance maximum at 482 nm, quantitatively converts these compounds to metastable 1,2-oxazepines, which thermally revert to the parent N-oxides and discharge the stored energy. The system achieves energy storage densities of up to 0.54 MJ/kg, comparable to Dewar anthracenes, while absorbing substantially more red-shifted light and offering nearly 3 orders of magnitude longer storage lifetimes of up to 1.4 years in the solid state. The thermal half-lives of the 1,2-oxazepines are tunable through para-substitution on the aryl ring and solvation, enabling up to a 1,300-fold reduction in half-life. Crucially, the 9-aryl substituent biases the transient oxaziridine intermediate toward selective reversion to the N-oxide over competing decomposition pathways, overcoming the limitations of other acridine N-oxides reported to date. This work establishes light-induced ring expansion as an effective strategy for MOST and expands the scope of viable MOST compounds.

title: Photomediated Chromium-Catalyzed Regio-, Diastereo-, and Enantioselective Deoxygenative Coupling of Activated Allylic and Propargylic Alcohols with Aldehydes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Chromium-catalyzed asymmetric Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction is a powerful tool for constructing synthetically valuable enantioenriched homoallylic alcohols and allenols. However, catalytic asymmetric NHK-type coupling of allylic or propargylic C–O electrophiles remains largely underdeveloped. Herein, we report a photomediated chromium-catalyzed deoxygenative coupling of activated allylic and propargylic alcohols with aldehydes, enabling the synthesis of a variety of chiral homoallylic alcohols with wide structural diversity and allenols. The reactions were performed under mild conditions, and a wide range of synthetically useful functional groups was found to be well tolerated. Importantly, this method provides a straightforward way for the construction of homoallylic alcohols bearing a chiral quaternary carbon center with high ee and dr. Furthermore, stereodivergent access to all four homoallylic alcohol stereoisomers is realized through orthogonal combinations of Z/E-configured allylic alcohols and R/S-configured ligands. Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies provided insight into the key catalytic intermediate and the origin of stereocontrol.

title: Hybrid Weakly Coordinated Solvents for Fast-Charging and Wide-Temperature Sodium-Ion Full Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The application of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) in wide-temperature and fast-charging scenarios is severely constrained by the performance limitations of electrolytes. Conventional ester-based electrolytes struggle to simultaneously achieve high ionic conductivity, low desolvation energy, and excellent interfacial stability. Herein, we propose a hybrid solvent system comprising ethyl propionate and ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN), aiming to synergistically enhance the rate capability and temperature adaptability of SIBs. The relatively weak coordination ability of both solvents effectively promotes anion participation in solvation structure, significantly lowering the Na+ desolvation energy barrier and inducing the formation of stable, inorganic-rich electrode/electrolyte interphases. Meanwhile, the dual-solvent combination increases the diversity of solvation configurations and reduces ion clustering, thereby enhancing ionic conductivity. The intrinsic nonflammability and excellent film-forming ability of PFPN further enhance safety and synergistically strengthen interfacial stability. Therefore, Prussian blue||hard carbon full cells operate stably over a wide temperature range from −50 to 100 °C. Notably, ampere-hour-level pouch cells deliver a capacity retention of 86.3% after 300 cycles at 25 °C and maintain stable operation for over 100 cycles even at −20 and 80 °C. This solvent synergy strategy offers a practical new pathway for the development of electrolytes for SIBs in extreme environments.

title: Functional Specialization of Coordination Spheres Enables Site-Selective Aromatic C–H Isotope Exchange in Ni Single-Atom Catalysts
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Engineering single-atom catalysts has predominantly focused on tailoring the primary coordination sphere, whereas whether distinct coordination spheres can be endowed with independent catalytic functions remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the functional specialization of coordination spheres by constructing a phosphorus-modified Ni–N2O2 single-atom catalyst for site-selective C–H deuteration. Advanced spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations show that phosphorus is incorporated outside the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination environment and support an O-linked phosphorus environment as a preferential second-sphere motif. This architecture decouples substrate recognition from catalytic activation. Specifically, second-sphere phosphorus selectively recognizes and anchors the amino group of haloanilines to dictate deuteration site selectivity, whereas the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination sphere promotes H2 activation and undergoes H2-assisted regeneration following D2O-induced hydroxylation, facilitated by P–O–Ni electronic communication, thereby sustaining efficient catalytic turnover. Consequently, the catalyst achieves highly site-selective C–H deuteration of chloro-, bromo-, and iodoanilines using H2 and D2O while completely preserving carbon–halogen bonds, whereas the phosphorus-free analogue exhibits negligible activity. This work identifies the structural origin and catalytic function of second-sphere phosphorus and establishes functional specialization of coordination spheres as a general design principle for independently programming substrate recognition and catalytic turnover in single-atom catalysis.

title: Magnetic Resonance Silent Activatable Probe with Massive Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated Fibrogenesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Biomarker-specific molecular imaging is vital in precision medicine. However, a fundamental challenge of most molecular imaging methods is the difficulty of distinguishing specific molecular signal from nonspecific signal arising from the distribution of the molecular probe. This is even more pronounced in metabolically active organs such as the kidney and liver where the probe may concentrate prior to elimination. As a result, almost all molecular imaging relies on delayed imaging to achieve specificity, but this constrains clinical throughput and impedes rapid assessment of the diseased organ. Here, we report a magnetic resonance (MR) probe, Fe(II)-IAFP2, which combines 3 drivers of relaxivity enhancement to decouple disease specificity from probe distribution. Fe(II)-IAFP2 is MR-silent in its Fe(II) state, producing negligible MR signal even at high concentrations. In inflammatory, fibrogenic microenvironments common to many diseases, rapid oxidation to Fe(III) activates MR enhancement, while reversible aldehyde-mediated binding to remodeled extracellular matrix further amplifies relaxivity and promotes retention at the site of tissue injury. This dual activation–retention mechanism enables robust signal generation within minutes of administration. In mouse models of renal and liver fibrogenesis, Fe(II)-IAFP2 generated disease-associated MR contrast within minutes after intravenous administration. Together, this work demonstrates an effective strategy for rapid, activity-based molecular MR imaging through the combination of pathological activation and complementary tissue retention.

title: Ammonia-Driven Nanoscale Surface Restructuring of Copper Catalysts during Nitrate Reduction Reaction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The electrolyte and applied potential are known to impact a catalyst’s structure and performance, yet the role of reaction intermediates and products in driving surface evolution remains largely unexplored. Here, using electrochemical atomic force microscopy, we show that the dynamic restructuring of copper (Cu) surfaces during nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) directly correlates with the rate and selectivity of ammonia (NH3) formation. At moderate overpotentials, where nitrite formation dominates, lateral expansion of Cu terraces is observed, whereas rapid NH3 formation at higher cathodic potentials induces Cu adislands enriched in low-coordinated step sites, revealing distinct restructuring pathways that accompany the transition from nitrite- to ammonia-selective NO3RR. These transformations are rationalized by an NH3-mediated Cu dissolution-redeposition mechanism. Our results identify reaction products as active modulators of catalyst surface structure, establishing a framework for understanding reaction-driven catalyst restructuring and enabling in situ control of catalyst surfaces through the interfacial reaction environment.

title: Acetaldehyde-Mediated Direct Conversion of Air to Nitric Acid
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The sustainable synthesis of nitric acid (HNO3) directly from air via N2 oxidation is a dream reaction but remains a long-standing challenge, owing to formidable thermodynamic and kinetic barriers. Here, we report a photoassisted thermocatalytic strategy in which acetaldehyde as a key medium enables efficient N2 oxidation to HNO3 under mild conditions. Acetaldehyde is oxidized to peracetic acid over 316L stainless steel, which subsequently generates radicals (CH3COOO•) under visible-light irradiation. These CH3COOO• radicals are highly reactive and can oxidize N2 at 200 °C and near-ambient pressures (1–5 bar), affording an HNO3 formation rate of 110.8 μmol h–1 with a concentration of 13,961 ppm and an N2 conversion of 0.45% within 2 h─approximately 2 to 4 orders of magnitude higher than previously reported systems. Notably, the kinetic irrelevance of H2O enables operation in a gas-phase flow configuration, allowing continuous and stable HNO3 production and gram-scale accumulation at the laboratory scale. This work introduces a groundbreaking reaction paradigm that couples organic radical chemistry and surface catalysis, offering a scalable and energy-efficient pathway for the green synthesis of HNO3.

title: A Molybdoenzyme Mediates Carbon–Sulfur Bond Making and Breaking in Ergothioneine Biosynthesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The molybdopterin-dependent ergothioneine synthase (MES) from Caldithrix abyssi is the first molybdoenzyme known to catalyze the formation of carbon–sulfur bonds. To complete its catalytic cycle, this bifunctional enzyme desulfurates l-cysteine at a pyridoxal 5′-phosphate binding site and transfers the harvested sulfur atom (S0) to the molybdenum center of a bis-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide cofactor more than 50 Å away. Subsequently, the sulfurated Mo-center transfers the labile sulfur atom onto the imidazole ring of Nα-trimethyl histidine (TMH). Combining experimental observations from cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, sequence-activity correlation, and substrate-specificity studies, we delineate the structural basis for long-distance sulfur transfer via a persulfide relay, the identity of the imidazole sulfurating species, and key sequence motifs that are indispensable for activity. Furthermore, the reversibility of MES-mediated sulfurization of TMH under physiological conditions suggests that ergothioneine may serve as a soluble reservoir of oxidizing equivalents, supporting anaerobic metabolism in deep-branching bacteria such as C. abyssi.

title: Empowering HFIP as a Radical Trifluoromethylating Reagent by Photoelectrochemical Iron Catalysis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The development of practical synthetic methods for incorporating trifluoromethyl (CF3) groups into organic scaffolds is of paramount importance in medicinal chemistry, as such modifications profoundly modulate the physicochemical properties of drug candidates. 1,1,1,3,3,3-Hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP) is widely utilized as a unique solvent in synthetic chemistry and also represents a promising CF3 source due to its high availability and low cost. Here we report an unprecedented photoelectrochemical iron-catalyzed protocol for radical trifluoromethylation that employs commercially accessible HFIP as the CF3 radical precursor. This method enables efficient trifluoromethylation of unactivated arenes, heteroarenes, and alkenes with a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance. Notably, this photoelectrocatalytic system is readily scalable for practical synthetic applications, and its utility has been demonstrated in the trifluoromethylation of peptides, allowing preferential modification of tryptophan residues in a chemoselective fashion.

title: General Synthesis of Functionalized 1,3-Diamines from Azoarenes and Enoates via Electrochemical Annulation and N–N Bond Cleavage Followed by Chemical Reduction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Despite the widespread utility of N-substituted 1,3-diamines across numerous fields, their selective synthesis directly from readily available feedstocks remains a long-standing challenge. In this context, we report a room-temperature electrochemical protocol for the synthesis of both symmetrical and unsymmetrical N,N′-disubstituted 1,3-diamines through electrochemical transformation of azoarenes with enoates, followed by convergent reduction of the resulting β-amino amides. This method features broad substrate scope, operational simplicity, no need for noble transition-metal catalysts, and high chemoselectivity. Mechanistic studies indicate that the reaction is initiated by the reduction of azoarenes, facilitated by HCOOH, while Zn2+ ions leached from anodic oxidation serve as a Lewis acid to promote intramolecular cyclization via ester amidation. Subsequent cathodic reduction drives N–N bond cleavage to afford the β-amino amide intermediates, thereby endowing azoarenes with dual-nitrogen synthon capability. This work provides a practical platform for the general synthesis of N,N′-difunctionalized 1,3-diamines and convenient late-stage structural editing of biomedicals.

title: A Double-Tethered Metallacyclobutadiene Catalyst for Cyclic Polymer Synthesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The synthesis, characterization, and catalytic polymerization results of an unprecedented double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complex (4) are discussed. Complex 4 is active for the polymerization of acetylenes. Complex 4 polymerizes tert-butylacetylene to form cyclic poly(tert-butylacetylene). Evidence for a cyclic polymer topology comes from size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and intrinsic viscosity (η) measurements. This unusual reactivity of complex 4 toward a tert-alkylacetylene is attributed to its fluxional behavior, which arises from the double tethering of an yne-ol proligand (2) that facilitates monomer access and catalytic turnover. The preliminary scope of this complex design is demonstrated through modification of the yne-ol proligand, which afforded two additional double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complexes 10 and 11 that are also catalytically active for polymerization.

title: Linker Steric Hindrance-Induced Defect Engineering Enables Oxygen Vacancy-Rich MOFs for Pollutant Degradation
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The widespread contamination of water by emerging contaminants (ECs) demands the development of efficient remediation technologies. Although advanced oxidation processes reliant on reactive oxygen species (ROS) show promise, they typically depend on energy- or reagent-intensive activation methods. Here, we introduce a linker steric hindrance-induced defect engineering (LSH-DE) strategy for metal–organic frameworks, which enables catalytic ROS generation using molecular oxygen (O2) as a benign terminal oxidant at ambient temperature and pressure. By systematically modulating the steric bulk of organic linkers, we precisely create missing-linker defects and direct the formation of oxygen vacancy (Vo) in robust Ce-UiO-66 during a rapid 15 min synthesis. Spectroscopic and computational analyses confirm that these oxygen vacancies promote O2 adsorption and activation to yield superoxide radicals (•O2–). The optimized catalyst, Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2, demonstrates superior activity in degrading ubiquitous ECs without requiring external energy inputs or chemical mediators. Furthermore, integration of Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2 into a membrane-based recirculating flow-through system enabled sustained water treatment, maintaining >90% BPA removal over 48 h with a high water permeance of 101.5 L m–2 h–1 bar–1. This work presents a general and sustainable approach for designing catalytic defects in MOFs, advancing the development of green, next-generation water purification technologies.

title: Mapping the Slow Propagation of Disorder across a Photoreceptor’s Tertiary Structure with Time-Resolved Crystallography
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Order–disorder transitions allow many proteins to shift between compact and flexible/unfolded states, thereby acting as structural switches that regulate catalysis, signaling, recognition, and allostery. We applied time-resolved serial oscillation crystallography to establish the structural kinetics of the light-triggered order–disorder transition of an animal-like cryptochrome as a six-second-long molecular movie with near-atomic all-residue spatial resolution and millisecond temporal resolution. Our 29 structural snapshots mapped the propagation of disorder across the tertiary structure motifs of a cryptochrome’s C-terminal region, triggered by a single broken D321–R492 salt bridge. The order–disorder transition followed a nucleation-propagation mechanism reminiscent of helix–coil dynamics and proceeded over up to five seconds, with regions distal to the D321–R492 trigger initially undergoing slow zero-order disordering before switching to first-order unfolding kinetics. Our per-residue density analysis provides a detailed structural-kinetic basis for understanding how order–disorder transitions emerge through directional propagation across protein tertiary structures, as occurring in signaling and many other biological systems.

title: Electron-Catalyzed Supramolecular Assembly with High Efficiency, Robustness, and Versatility
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Although catalysis is widely exploited by nature to orchestrate noncovalent supramolecular assembly and build up complex living systems, its utilization in synthetic chemistry has conventionally been limited to accelerating covalent reactions. Consequently, the development of artificial systems for catalytic assembly remains a formidable and largely unexplored challenge. Here, we present a rationally designed strategy of electron-catalyzed supramolecular assembly, wherein the electron acts as an efficient, robust, and versatile catalyst to accelerate the formation of a donor–acceptor complex. Optimization of the elementary steps and intermediate stability yields an efficient catalytic cycle, furnishing the process with both a high turnover number and operational robustness in open air. Furthermore, the electron catalysis can be readily triggered by diverse external stimuli─including electricity, light, and mechanical force─enabling precise spatiotemporal control over the assembly process and near-quantitative synthesis of supramolecular complexes. Collectively, this work establishes a well-elucidated strategy of catalytic assembly with remarkable practicality, advancing the frontiers of noncovalent synthetic chemistry.

title: Role of (Co)substrate Coordination to Iron in Activating Its Two-Electron Reduction of Dioxygen: Mechanism of Pterin Activation in Tryptophan Hydroxylase
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Many O2-activating mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes require substrate or cofactor/cosubstrate coordination to iron to form the key peroxy-bridged intermediate necessary for catalysis with no net change in the iron redox state. The role of (co)substrate coordination, however, remained unclear. Here, we leverage a pterin-dependent enzyme, tryptophan hydroxylase, for which cosubstrate (pterin) coordination can be experimentally controlled by the absence and presence of substrate, to explicitly determine the role of pterin coordination in O2 binding and peroxo formation. EPR, absorption, circular dichroism, and magnetic circular dichroism spectroscopies on the {FeNO}7 analog of the unobservable {FeO2}8 intermediate without and with pterin coordination demonstrate that pterin coordination induces new absorption bands and enhances NO affinity by 3.6 kcal mol–1 at 277 K. These new bands are pterin-to-iron ligand-to-metal charge-transfer transitions that compensate the electron donation from iron to NO upon NO binding. Extension of our findings on {FeNO}7 to {FeO2}8 evidences that pterin coordination stabilizes O2 binding and facilitates the two-electron transfer from pterin to {FeO2}8 to reduce the transition-state barrier for peroxo formation by 12.7 kcal mol–1, corresponding to a 1010 increase in reaction rate. The electron transfer pathways established herein underscore a unified mechanism for the pterin-dependent, α-ketoglutarate-dependent, extradiol, and intradiol dioxygenase families of mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes through which (co)substrate coordination enhances O2 binding via one-electron transfer within {FeO2}8 and two-electron donation from the (co)substrate (one to bound O2 and one to iron) to generate the peroxo species with no net redox change on the iron.

title: A Crystalline LaCl3 Reinforced Amorphous Oxyhalide Electrolyte for Thermally Stable All-Solid-State Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are a promising next-generation energy storage technology, but their development is often constrained by the thermal instability and high cost of solid-state electrolytes (SSEs). Amorphous oxyhalide electrolytes, while mechanically deformable, are particularly susceptible to thermal degradation. Here, we report a novel and cost-effective composite SSE fabricated by embedding LaCl3 nanocrystals within an amorphous Li–Al–O–Cl (LAOC) matrix. This unique architecture synergistically combines the high ionic conductivity of the amorphous phase with the enhanced thermal and mechanical robustness imparted by the crystalline phase. The resulting Li–La–Al–O–Cl electrolyte achieves a high room-temperature ionic conductivity exceeding 1 mS cm–1 and demonstrates exceptional thermal stability, remaining a solid powder at 150 °C, a temperature at which the baseline LAOC melts. This enhanced thermal and thermo-mechanical integrity, combined with excellent deformability, enables superior interfacial contact and stability with cathodes. The Li–La–Al–O–Cl-based ASSBs maintain stable operation at 80 °C, in stark contrast to the rapid failure of LAOC-based cells. This strategy of reinforcing a soft amorphous matrix with a rigid crystalline offers a new pathway for designing thermally robust, high-performance, and commercially viable SSEs.

title: Molecular Mechanophores Based on Stress-Enhanced Exciton Transition between Phosphorescent Probes and Polymer Matrix
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Mechanophores provide an in situ and remote tool for quantifying invisible stress in polymers by photonic signals, offering distinct advantages for stress distribution analysis of large-area surfaces and instrument-free stress observation. However, achieving an ideal mechanophore that integrates with sensitive, reversible, and molecular-level stress sensing is attractive yet challenging. Here, we report practical guidance for developing ideal mechanophores that promote the molecular probe’s exciton transition for room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) under stress, through the “assisted lowest triplet (T1) state” of the adjacent polymer chain.
